forClaude:
This file is the lesson plan for a video that teaches **VeinScript**, written with its author. Use it to help write the narration, slides, on-screen text and the order of the demos, and to answer questions about the language.

1. **The code here is real.** Every block was cut from a sample that compiles today, by a generator, not typed by hand. When you write new VeinScript, copy the syntax you see here exactly. If a construct does not appear here or in `ALL-SAMPLES.md`, say you are not sure instead of inventing one.
2. **It is not a C-family language.** It has no `!=`, no `!`, no `for`/`in`, no `class`, no semicolons and no `::`. See *What VeinScript deliberately does not have*.
3. **A newline ends a statement.** Continue a line with a *trailing* `+` or `,`, and keep `} else {` on one line.
4. **Never present these as working:** `use` (retired, so write `need "Author.Bundle"`), `sync`, `count`, `map<K,V>`, `on` and `transform`. They are lexed but have no implementation. An event's full name is `Author.Bundle.Name`, and it is never unified by bare name.
5. **The lesson order is deliberate.** Each lesson only uses what came before it. Lessons marked ★ are the core path, which works on its own as one complete first video.
6. **Output blocks are real** and were captured by running the sample. Interactive samples (consoles, networks, servers) have no captured output. The presenter runs those live.
pitch: VeinScript is a language where the building block of a program isn't an object or a function. It's an identity. You declare the data an identity can carry, called shapes and written with a dollar sign. You declare the tags it can wear, called marks and written with a hash. And you declare the messages it can send, called events and written with an at sign. All behaviour lives in shards, and a shard never calls anything. It targets every identity that matches and acts on each one. When two shards write the same field in the same tick, the field itself says how the writes combine, for example 'folds sum', so the order the shards run in never matters. The same model runs a game loop, a chat across three console windows, and a website assembled from fragments. It comes with one compiler, an interpreter and a C# backend, plus a desktop IDE that lets you step through time and watch your identities change one tick at a time.
mentalModel:
**Everything is an identity.** Behaviour never calls behaviour. A program makes identities with `spawn()` and hangs data and tags on them. Behaviour then *finds* them with a query.

- **Shape `$Health`**: the fields an identity carries (a component), e.g. `attach $Health to e { hp: 5 }`.
- **Mark `#Enemy`**: a tag with no fields, e.g. `mark e #Enemy` / `unmark`. `$Enemy` and `#Enemy` are two different things.
- **Event `@Damaged`**: a message with a payload. `emit` queues it and `hear @Damaged as d { … }` reacts to it. Every event carries provenance (`d.from.name`, `d.cause`).
- **Shard**: the only place behaviour lives. It is a set of blocks: `run once`, `each tick`, `settled`, `every N`, `hear @E`. Inside a block, `target $Health #Enemy as self { … }` visits every identity that carries all of those.
- **SF / fn**: an `SF` is a named sequence of emits and never returns. An `fn` computes a value and returns it.
- **Builder + bring**: a template. The *name of its output field* decides what it makes: `markup`→`@Html`, `css`→`@Style`, `code`→`@Script`, `line`→`@Print`, and no output field→`@BuilderName`. A `mark` member makes it an identity template, so `bring Unit(10, 6)` does spawn + attach + mark. `$Shape` includes copy a shape's fields into the parameter list, and arguments bind by position.
- **Bundle**: the module, written `bundle Game by you { … }`. Everything in it is private by default. Only `shared("…")` members of a `publicator` can be used from another bundle, either as `*Author.Bundle.Publicator.member` or as a bare name after `need "Author.Bundle"`. An `app` manifest `load`s bundles. The first one is the principal, and its `start @E` is the only boot event. The others join the same runtime.

**Time: tick → commit → settled.**
1. `run once` seeds the world.
2. Every `each tick` block runs. A write to a field is a *contribution*, and the shape says how contributions merge. With `hp: int folds sum`, two shards that each do `hp -= 1` give `hp - 2`, whatever order they ran in.
3. `spawn` happens immediately. `attach`/`unattach`/`mark`/`unmark`/`destroy` wait for the commit point, so no shard ever sees a half-changed world.
4. `settled` runs after the folds are reconciled. That is where you read final values, such as death checks.

Events drain one at a time. Each event's structural changes are committed before the next event runs, so the next event sees what the last one built. Inside the event that made a change, the change is not visible yet.

**Two execution models, one identity model.** The reactive loop covers `emit`/`hear`/`ShardView` → `@Response`, console and network. The ECS tick loop covers `target`/`each tick`/`settled`/`folds` and is driven by `--ticks N`. Both run in the interpreter. The identity half also compiles to C# with `veinc emit`.

sigils.meaning: Data an identity carries, as fields (a component). `attach $Health to e { hp: 5 }`
A tag with no fields. `mark e #Enemy`, `unmark e #Enemy`
A message with a payload. `emit` queues it and `hear @Damaged as d { … }` reacts
A template, referenced by name, e.g. `*Vein.Web.Elements.&Heading(…)`. A local one is used as `bring Unit(10, 6)`

lessons.title: Two shards, one `hp`
lessons.goal: Read a complete VeinScript program: shapes carry data, marks tag identities, shards `target` every match, and `folds sum` merges writes made in the same tick.
lessons.hook: Two pieces of code, neither knows the other exists, and both subtract one from the same number in the same frame. In most languages one write wins or you reach for a lock. Here the number drops by exactly two, every time, whichever runs first.
say: `shape $Health` declares data an identity can carry, and `hp: int folds sum` says what happens when several shards write `hp` in one tick: their deltas are added.
`run once` seeds the world. Inside `repeat 3`, `spawn()` makes a new identity, `attach $Health to e { hp: 5 }` gives it data, and `mark e #Enemy` tags it. `$` means shape, `#` means mark.
Drain and Poison are two separate shards with the same line: `target $Health #Enemy as self { self.Health.hp -= 1 }`. Neither calls the other, and neither knows the other exists.
`target` is the loop over identities: it visits every identity carrying both `$Health` and `#Enemy`, and `self.Health.hp` reads that identity's field.

The Undertaker reads `hp` in `settled`, which runs after the tick's writes are reconciled, so the value it sees is final. At zero or below it does `mark self #Dead` and `unmark self #Enemy`. `Entity` is the id of the identity the loop is on.
Run it for three ticks: every enemy prints hp 3, then 1, then -1, then 'died'. That is 5 minus 2 per tick, so both writes landed.

Live: delete `folds sum` and run again. Now hp falls by only one per tick, so a write was silently lost, and `veinc exec` on the edited file flags a Drain x Poison conflict on `$Health.hp`. Put `folds sum` back.

show.caption: Data, a seeded world, and two shards writing the same field
Reading the result after the tick settles

gotchas: Use `veinc run … --ticks 3` on camera. The header's `veinc render` line prints an emit trace instead of the hp lines.
Removing `folds sum` still passes `veinc check`. Only the run and `veinc exec` show the lost write, so rehearse the edit on a copy.
Read a `folds` field in `settled`. A mid-tick read is not reconciled yet (RULES 13).
`#Enemy` and `#Dead` are never declared, so their names go unchecked and a typo would silently create a new mark (RULES 16).
With no `spawn()` the world is empty and every `target` matches nothing (RULES 10).
The lines print through `emit *Vein.Console.Io.@Print`. Don't explain it yet: l04 reveals that printing is an event.

lessons.title: `bring`: one line per identity
lessons.goal: Declare an identity template with `builder … { $Shape   mark #Mark }` and create identities with `bring`, including `bring N`.
lessons.hook: Last lesson took three lines to make one enemy: spawn, attach, mark. A builder does it in one line. `bring Mob(12)` lowers to exactly those three statements, and `bring Unit(12, 6)` to four, with one attach per shape.
say: `builder Unit { $Health $Shield   mark #Unit }` has no body. The shapes and the mark it lists are its whole definition.
The `mark` member makes it an identity template: `bring Unit(12, 6)` means spawn, attach `$Health` with hp 12, attach `$Shield` with sp 6, and mark `#Unit`.
Arguments bind by position across the includes in declaration order: `$Health` takes hp, then `$Shield` takes sp. `Mob` and `Ward` include one shape each, so they take one argument.
`bring 2 Unit(4, 2)` makes two separate identities, e4 and e5, not one shared one.

Wear targets `$Health $Shield #Unit`, and several shapes in one query is an AND. After tick one e1 reads `hp=11 sp=4`, while e2 (a Mob) and e3 (a Ward) never change, because neither carries both shapes.
Live: `veinc scaffold samples/entities_template.vein Unit` prints a ready-to-paste `bring Unit(` call with one slot per field, each labelled with its type and the shape it came from.

show.caption: Two shapes, three one-line templates, and a shard that uses them

gotchas: Without a `mark` member, or a mark carried by an included shape (RULES 15c), a `$Shape` include only copies fields. `bring Mob(12)` then emits `@Mob`, attaches nothing, and `target $Health` never sees it. `veinc check` warns VS0237 when nothing hears that event (RULES 8).

Ask `veinc scaffold` for the argument order instead of counting (RULES 9). Keep the header's scaffold listing off screen: it shows `?` slots, while the real command prints `base, // hp: int from $Health REQUIRED — give it a value`.
`bring 2 Unit(…) as n` is VS0222, because a count cannot be combined with `as` (RULES 7b).
A builder's output field decides what it makes, and a `mark` member makes an identity (RULES 5, 7).
lessons.next: Now the timing question from lesson one: when exactly does a `mark`, an `unmark` or a `destroy` take effect?

lessons.title: Nothing changes mid-frame
lessons.goal: Predict when structural changes land: `spawn` is immediate, while attach, unattach, mark, unmark and destroy wait for the commit point, and `settled` sees the result.
lessons.hook: Three shards remove things this frame, and a fourth, running in the same frame, counts what's left. It sees nothing removed, and that is the guarantee, not a bug.
say: `mark #Alive` and `mark #Guarded` on their own lines, outside any shard, declare the two marks. Lesson 1 never declared `#Enemy`. Declaring any mark makes the compiler check mark names in this bundle, and lesson 11 comes back to that. `builder Mob { $Health, $Shield   mark #Alive   mark #Guarded }`: each of the three `bring Mob(…)` calls gives an identity both shapes and both marks, with hp 10, 20 and 30.
Three removal verbs of three sizes: Cull does `unmark m #Alive` under 15 hp, Disarm does `unattach $Shield from m`, and Reap does `destroy m` over 25 hp.

During counts in `each tick`, the same phase as the removals, using `var alive = 0` counters. `var` declares a local you reassign (`alive = alive + 1`), while lesson 1's `let e = spawn()` names a value you don't mean to change (the compiler does not enforce that today). After runs the identical counts in `settled`.
Frame 1 prints `during   alive 3   shielded 3   entities 3`, then `after    alive 1   shielded 0   entities 2`. Every removal was queued and landed together at the commit point.
The 10-hp mob still exists, it just isn't `#Alive`. The 30-hp one is gone completely. That's why `entities` is 2 and `alive` is 1.
Live: cut shard During, paste it above Cull, and run again. The numbers don't change: no shard ever sees a half-changed world, so shard order can't matter.
Live in the Workbench: open the file, go to the Runtime panel, press Boot, then Step ▸ once, and watch the entity browser go from three identities to two.

show.caption: Three mobs, each with two shapes and two marks
unmark, unattach, destroy: one shard each
The same count, during the tick and after it

gotchas: attach, unattach, mark, unmark and destroy are DEFERRED to the commit point. `destroy m` does not make `m` vanish mid-frame (RULES 11).
A structural change is invisible inside the phase or event that made it, so seed worlds in `run once` and read in a later phase (RULES 12, 12b).
A mark-only query such as `target #Alive as a` is VS0236. Name a shape too, as `target $Health #Alive as a` does.
Frames 2 and 3 both print 'alive 1 shielded 0 entities 2', because nothing is left to remove.
There is no `!=` or `!`: write `not (a == b)` and `not x` (RULES 2).
lessons.next: Everything so far has run on a clock. Most programs react to something instead, like a typed line or a request, and every line we've printed was already an event.

lessons.part: First video: events, failure and apps
lessons.title: Printing was an event all along
lessons.goal: Write a reactive program: name and declare a boot event, `hear` events with an `as` binding, and `emit` events with payloads.
lessons.hook: Every line we've printed so far was an `emit`. Nothing in VeinScript calls the terminal. The terminal is just another listener.
say: `bundle App { … }` wraps the whole program. A bundle is VeinScript's module (lessons 1-3 had one too, just off-screen), and with no `by` in its header (compare `bundle Store by you {`) its author is `local`. Inside it, `start @Boot { }` names the entry event, `event @Boot { }` declares it, and `veinc run` fires it once.
Shard Main is only two `hear` blocks, with no `run once` and no `each tick`. Unlike the clock-driven shards so far, it does nothing until an event arrives.

`emit *Vein.Console.Io.@Print { text: … }` writes a line, and `hear *Vein.Console.Io.@Input as i` fires once for each line you type. Nothing writes to stdout or reads stdin directly: even the `print` helper you'll see in lesson 5 is an SF that just emits @Print.
Read the path left to right: `*` starts it, `Vein` is the author, `Console` the bundle, `Io` the publicator, and `@Print` the event.
`as i` binds the payload, so `i.text` is the typed line, and `+` joins strings.
Live: run it, type `hello` and get `you said hello`, type one more line, then end with Ctrl+Z and Enter on Windows (Ctrl+D on Unix).

show.caption: A whole interactive program: one entry event, one shard, two handlers

gotchas: A newline ends a statement. If you wrap `"you said " + i.text`, the `+` must END the first line (RULES 1).
A string literal stays on one line (RULES 3).

`start @Boot { }` alone is enough today: delete `event @Boot { }` and `veinc check` still says ok and the run looks the same. Keep the declaration anyway, because it is what makes @Boot show up in `veinc events samples/console.vein`, which lists no events without it.
Piping empty input ends the run right after the prompt, because the run stops at stdin EOF. Type live in a real terminal.
The old `use Console` form is retired (VS0338). Stdlib names are reached by `*` path or with `need "Author.Bundle"` (RULES 18).
lessons.next: Shards can't call each other, so where does reusable logic go? Into two kinds of function, split by what they produce.

lessons.part: First video: events, failure and apps
lessons.title: `fn` computes, `SF` emits
lessons.goal: Choose between `fn` (returns a value) and `SF` (a named sequence of emits), and call shared ones from another bundle by qualified path.
lessons.hook: VeinScript has functions, two kinds of them, and the split is not about syntax. It's about what they produce: a value, or events.
say: `fn bonus(streak: int) return int` computes and returns, so it can go anywhere a value can. Parameters are written `name: Type`.
`SF announce(label: string, value: int)` has no return type, and its body is an `emit`. An SF is a named emit sequence, and a call to it stands alone as a statement.
`fib` is a local `fn` that recurses. It needs no `shared` to be called inside this bundle.
`shared("…")` inside a `publicator` is the only thing that crosses a bundle boundary, and the string is a label shown in completion.
Scoreboard calls `announce("fib(10)", fib(10))`, an fn result passed into an SF call, and the output reads `fib(10): 55` after `streak 3 bonus: 15` and `streak 99 bonus: 50`.

Across bundles: `*Vein.Math.Scalars.clamp(99.0, 0.0, 10.0)` is Vein.Math's shared fn and prints `clamp(99, 0, 10) = 10`, and `*Vein.Console.Io.print(…)` is Vein.Console's shared SF, which emits @Print for you.

show.caption: A shared fn, a shared SF, and a local recursive fn
Four kinds of call: local and cross-bundle, fn and SF

gotchas: `-> T` on an SF is VS0105, and `return` outside an fn is VS0107 (SYNTAX-DECISIONS D6).
Only `shared("…")` inside a publicator crosses a bundle boundary (RULES 17). A label over 160 characters warns VS0243 (RULES 17d).
An SF's emits queue. They do not print at the moment of the call (RULES 21).
Whole floats print without `.0`, so clamp shows `10`, not `10.0`.
lessons.next: An SF names a sequence of emits. Put many emitters together and you get a web page that no function returns: shards each emit a fragment.

lessons.part: First video: events, failure and apps
lessons.title: A website assembled from events
lessons.goal: Serve a site with several routes and a form, where shards contribute `@Html` fragments per route and a `ShardView` assembles the response.
lessons.hook: No handler in this site returns a page. Shards emit fragments, one view listens, and the page is whatever arrived.
say: `need "Vein.Web"` makes the stdlib builders `Heading`, `Paragraph` and `Link` usable by bare name. None of them has a `mark` member. Each has a `markup = …` output field instead, and a builder's output field name decides what it makes. So `bring Heading("Say hello")` spawns no identity and writes no markup: it queues an @Html fragment. A `css` field would make @Style, `code` @Script and `line` @Print.
Routing is a plain `if r.path == "/greet"`. Every page shard hears every @Request and only contributes when its path matches.
Same path, two methods. On GET, Greet brings a heading, emits the form as a raw `@Html` string and links home. On POST it reads the submitted field as `r.who`, an ordinary payload field.
Router emits @Render and is declared after the page shards, so @Render queues behind every fragment. ShardView Page appends each `h.markup` to `var html` and answers @Response when @Render arrives.
`if not (html == "")`: no fragments means no response, and the server turns that into a 404. There is no `!=` in the language.
Live: `veinc serve samples/web_site.vein --port 8080`, open http://localhost:8080/, click 'say hello', submit `Ada` and get 'Hello Ada', then try /nope for the 404.

show.caption: One `need` brings in the web vocabulary
One route, two methods: the form and its answer
@Render queues last; the view assembles or stays silent

gotchas: Don't read out the comment at lines 63-64. It's stale: Vein.Web's @Request has no `?`, and form and query values simply arrive as extra payload fields.

The form is one string literal, and a literal cannot span lines (RULES 3). A `+` at the start of the next line would begin a new statement (RULES 1). To wrap it, end the line with `+`, which also works inside the emit payload.
`bring` and `emit` queue. A view answering @Request directly would see an empty page, which is why Router exists and must stay below the page shards (RULES 21).
`veinc serve` gives every request a fresh interpreter, so nothing persists between visits (RULES 22).
Offline fallback: `veinc render samples/web_site.vein /greet --set method=POST --set who=Ada` prints Hello Ada. Under Git Bash, set MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 for `/` arguments (RULES 23).
lessons.next: Something will go wrong in a program like this, such as a bad row or a divide by zero, and there's no try/catch to reach for.

lessons.title: No try/catch: failure is a message
lessons.goal: Collect every diagnostic in a program with one `hear`, raise your own with info/warn/error, and see a runtime fault stop only its own block.
lessons.hook: I'm going to divide by zero on purpose, and the program keeps going.
say: Collector is the catch: `hear *Vein.Diagnostics.Report.@DiagnosticRaised as d`. `d.severity` is an int (0 info, 1 warning, 2 error), and Collector prints each with its own prefix: note, WARN, ERROR.
A catch belongs to the code that failed, but a `hear` belongs to whoever cares. Collector gets every diagnostic in the program, and no failing shard knows it exists.
Validate brings a row with an empty title and rank -1, then calls `*Vein.Diagnostics.Report.info`, `warn` and `error`. Nothing failed here: the program made a judgement and reported it.
Compute evaluates `5 % 0`, a remainder by zero, and the runtime raises the same event: `ERROR | Compute (once): Attempted to divide by zero.` It names the shard and the phase.
The block stops, not just the statement: 'THIS LINE NEVER PRINTS' never prints. Carry_on still runs in `settled` and prints '-- the program is still alive --' and both rows.
The collected lines appear after the plain prints because Collector answers with another @Print, which joins the back of the same queue.

show.caption: The catch: one hear for every diagnostic in the program
Diagnostics you raise yourself
A real fault stops its block; the rest of the program carries on

gotchas: Don't repeat the header's 'the same six lines still appear'. This run prints four diagnostic lines: three raised and one fault.
Carry_on is in `settled` because the rows brought in Validate's `run once` commit at the end of that phase. Another `run once` block would see nothing (RULES 12b).
emit queues, so the Collector's lines arrive one hop after an inline @Print (RULES 21).
Validate reports but does not reject. Both rows still exist and are printed.
A file or network failure is a message too: @FileMissing, @Failed, @Undelivered (RULES 28b).
lessons.next: Collector heard an event from Vein.Diagnostics, a bundle it never wired up by hand. The same mechanism lets a whole program be several bundles sharing one queue.

lessons.part: First video: events, failure and apps
lessons.title: An app is a list of capabilities
lessons.goal: Link several bundles into one runtime with an `app` manifest, where only the principal boots and the others react across bundles.
lessons.hook: Delete one line of this manifest and the app stops invoicing, without touching a single other file.
say: `app Shop` loads three bundles. The first `load` is the principal, and Store's `start @Ordered { item: "widget", qty: 3 }` is the app's single boot event.
Store shares `@Ordered` and `@Shipped` from `publicator Orders`. Inside its own bundle it just writes `@Shipped`.
Billing declares no `start`. It hears `*you.Store.Orders.@Shipped` (author, bundle, publicator, event) and emits its own shared `@Invoiced`.
The manifest comment says Audit, the third `load`, watches both of the others. All three bundles share one event queue.
Run it: the banner reads `principal 'Store' boots; 3 bundle(s) linked into one runtime`, then Store, Audit, Billing and Audit print in queue order.
Live: comment out `load "Billing.vein"` and run again. Invoicing disappears, Audit still sees the order, and no other file changed.

show.caption: The whole app: three loads, the first one boots
The principal: shared events and the one start
A capability: no start, it only reacts

gotchas: Declare a cross-bundle event with `shared("…")` inside a publicator. That's the bundle's API (RULES 17). Only `veinc symbols` checks it, with VS0305 on an unshared `*you.Store.Orders.@Shipped`. `veinc check` and `veinc run` don't, and Billing still hears an unshared @Shipped.
An event's identity is Author.Bundle.Name, so other bundles write `*you.Store.Orders.@Shipped` (RULES 20).
Read the output as a queue, not a call stack: '[Audit] saw order' prints before '[Billing] invoicing' (RULES 21).
Only the principal's `start` fires. A `start` in any other loaded bundle does not (VS0331). Older LANGUAGE.md text says every bundle boots, which is wrong.
lessons.next: That's the whole model in one sitting. The deep dives start with everyday code: four loops, and no `for`.

lessons.title: Four loops, and no `for`
lessons.goal: Pick the right loop (`while`, `repeat N as i`, `target <list> as x`, `target $Shape #Mark as e`) and use `break` and `continue` in all four.
lessons.hook: There's no `for` and no `in` in VeinScript. There are four loops instead, and each one says what it's walking.
say: `while i < 10` with `continue` at 2 and `break` at 5 prints 1, 3, 4.
`repeat 3 as r` counts from 0, and `r` is the same number the built-in `Index` gives: 'repeat r=0 Index=0'.
A count is a limit, not a promise: `break` at `r == 2` stops `repeat 10` after 'capped r=0' and 'capped r=1'.
`words("alpha beta skip gamma")` returns a list and `target … as w` walks it. `continue` skips "skip", so three words are numbered.
The fourth loop is the identity loop in Report: `target $Score #Player as p` with the same `continue`. Make brings Ada 30, Grace 20 and Alan 10, and Alan's 10 points never print.
Report runs in `each tick`, not in Make's `run once`, because a bring commits at the phase boundary. With `--ticks 2` the two score lines print twice.

show.caption: while, repeat, and a loop over a list
The identity loop, with the same continue

gotchas: `for`, `in` and `loop` are refused on purpose (SYNTAX-DECISIONS D3).
There is no `!=`: inequality is `not (a == b)` (RULES 2).
A `target` in the same `run once` as the brings would find nothing (RULES 11, 12b).
The comment above Report says 'This is the second tick'. It means the phase after `run once`, and Report prints on tick 1 too.
`Index` is the nearest loop's 0-based counter (RULES 14c).
lessons.next: Loops walk data. The next thing most programs need is a state that changes over time, and a clean way to branch on it.

lessons.title: A state machine with `enum` and `match`
lessons.goal: Declare an enum inside the shape that owns it, advance it by comparing cases, and read it back with `match … when … else`.
lessons.hook: An enum in VeinScript lives inside the data it describes. There's no top-level enum at all.
say: `enum State { Kickoff, Play, Over }` is declared inside `shape $Match`, and `state: State` types the field.
`bring Referee(State.Kickoff, 0)`: a case is a value you can pass around, bound by position (state, then clock).
Each tick, Whistle bumps the clock, moves Kickoff to Play, and moves Play to Over once `m.Match.clock >= 3`. Logic is written in words, like `and`.
Commentary reads the state back in `settled` with `match m.Match.state { when Kickoff … when Play … when Over … else … }`.

The output is t1 in play, t2 in play, t3 full time, t4 full time. 'awaiting kickoff' never prints because Whistle moved on in frame 1 before settled ran, and 'NO STATE' never prints either. That absence is the check.

show.caption: An enum inside its shape, advanced each tick, read back with match

gotchas: A top-level `enum` is VS0102 by design (SYNTAX-DECISIONS D11).
SAMPLES.md §3 still lists `enum` as lexed but unimplemented, and match_orders.vein's header says an enum case can't be a value. This file runs and is in check-backend, so don't repeat either claim.
`when` only exists inside `match`. There is no `when cond { }` conditional (SYNTAX-DECISIONS D2).

A misspelt case in a value, like `State.Kikoff`, is VS0242 at the spelling. A misspelt `when` arm is not checked: `when Paly` compiles clean and never matches, so t1 and t2 print NO STATE. The `else` arm is what catches it.
A match arm may start its own line, unlike `} else {` after an `if` (RULES 2b).
lessons.next: `match` branches on a value. Marks are the other way to sort identities into kinds, and they stay on an identity across ticks.

lessons.title: `$Enemy` and `#Enemy`: marks are tags that stay
lessons.goal: Declare marks, combine several in a query, swap them at runtime, and know that declaring marks turns on name checking.
lessons.hook: This file gives a shape and a mark the exact same name, on purpose.
say: `mark #Enemy`, `mark #Awake` and `mark #Spent` at the top declare the marks. Declaring any mark switches on name checking for this bundle.
`shape $Enemy { hp: int folds sum }` is data, and `#Enemy` is a tag. Same word, different sigil, two different things: Seed attaches one and marks the other.
Drain targets `$Enemy #Enemy #Awake`, so it needs the shape and both marks. Several marks in one query are an AND.
Reaper, in `settled`, marks `#Spent` and unmarks `#Awake` and `#Enemy` once hp hits 0, so that enemy leaves Drain's query.
Ledger matches only `#Spent`. Run five ticks: tick three prints each 'spent' line, and from tick four on only 'ledger: eN is spent' lines appear. The tag stayed on the identity.
Live: misspell `#Enemy` as `#Enmey` in Drain's target and `veinc check` warns VS0218, because the mark isn't declared.

show.caption: Declared marks, a same-named shape, a two-mark query
Swap tags when hp runs out; the kept tag persists

gotchas: The header says `--ticks 3`, which never prints a ledger line: marks set in tick 3's `settled` commit only after it (RULES 11). Use `--ticks 5`.
VS0218 only fires in a bundle that declares at least one mark. A bundle with no declared marks silently accepts typos (RULES 16).
`$Enemy` and `#Enemy` are different things (RULES 15).

Use the bare `#Mark` in target/mark/unmark. A qualified `*Author.Bundle.Publicator.#Mark` after a shape in a target is error VS0100 ('Expected 'as', found Star'), and in mark/unmark it is VS0100 ('Expected member name'). The quiet case is worse: `target *Vein.Audio.Sound.#Audible as a { … }` on its own passes `veinc check` and matches nothing, because it is read as a loop over a collection. That is the 'parses and resolves to nothing' trap in RULES 17b.
lessons.next: `$Enemy` and `#Enemy` shared a word. One word can go further and name four things at once.

lessons.title: One word, four sigils
lessons.goal: Read `$`, `#`, `@` and the bare builder name as part of a name, and see `$Switch`, `#Switch`, `@Switch` and `Switch` coexist.
lessons.hook: This file declares `Switch` four times, and none of them collide.
say: `shape $Switch` is data, `mark #Switch` is a tag, `event @Switch` is a message, and `builder Switch` is the template. Inside its own bundle a builder is normally written bare, as in `bring Switch(1)`. Its sigil `&` shows up in a qualified path, as in `bring *Vein.Console.Io.&Console(…)`, and when you name it to a tool: `veinc scaffold samples/sigil_names.vein '&Switch'` prints the bring call, while a bare `Switch` there gives the `@Switch` emit body.
`builder Switch { $Switch   mark #Switch }` uses the word three times and means something different each time.
`bring Switch(1)` and `bring Switch(0)` spawn two identities with `on` set to 1 and 0.
In `settled`, Flip targets `$Switch #Switch as s` and emits `@Switch { n: s.Switch.on }`. Listen hears `@Switch as e` and prints `e.n`.

Output order: '$Switch #Switch matched 2' prints before the two '@Switch says' lines even though Flip runs first. Report queues its @Print straight from `settled`, while each @Switch line needs one more hop: Flip's @Switch is queued, Listen hears it, and only then queues its @Print, behind Report's.

show.caption: Shape, mark, event and builder, all named Switch

gotchas: `on` works here only as a field name. The `on` keyword is lexed but not implemented: `on click { }` is VS0103.
`$Enemy` and `#Enemy` are different things, and the same holds for all four Switch declarations (RULES 15).

The brings commit when `run once` ends, so no `target` inside any shard's `run once` sees them. From the first tick on, `each tick` and `settled` both see them, so `settled` is a choice here and not a requirement (RULES 11, 12b).
emit queues, so Listen's lines land after Report's (RULES 21).
lessons.next: Builders make identities, but `bring` hasn't handed anything back so far. What if one identity needs to point at another?

lessons.title: `bring … as`: pointing at what you built
lessons.goal: Bind the identity a template spawned with `bring X(…) as name` and store it in an `Entity`-typed field.
lessons.hook: An identity is a value. Name it when you build it, and you can store it inside another identity.
say: `shape $Edge { to: Entity, weight: int folds sum }`: `Entity` is a field type.
`bring Node("hub")  as hub` names the identity it spawned. `as` means the same thing here as in `target … as` and `hear … as`.
`hub` and `leaf` are ordinary values: `bring Edge(hub,  1)` passes one as the first argument, which fills `to`.
Report prints 'edge e3 -> e1 w=1', 'edge e4 -> e2 w=2' and 'edge e5 -> e1 w=3', so the stored ids are real. The `e` comes from the string literal, and an Entity itself prints as a number.
`mark #Node` and `mark #Edge` are declared, so this bundle's mark names are checked.

show.anchor: shape $Edge { to: Entity, weight: int folds sum }
show.caption: Named nodes, edges that store them, and the proof

gotchas: `as` on a fragment builder is VS0221, and `as` with a count (`bring 3 Node(…) as n`) is VS0222 (RULES 7b).
Arguments bind positionally: `Edge(hub, 1)` fills `to`, then `weight` (RULES 9).
`settled` runs once per tick, so `--ticks 2` prints the edge and node lines twice.
Declaring any mark turns on name checking for the whole bundle (RULES 16).
lessons.next: Every query so far came back in spawn order. Next, reading the same identities in an order you choose, and numbering them as you go.

lessons.title: `target … by` and `Index`: order and position
lessons.goal: Sort a query at read time with `by Shape.field` (ascending, stable, ordinal), and number, cut off and stripe rows with `Index`.
lessons.hook: Five rows, brought in scrambled order. The same rows print in three different orders in one frame, and not one id moves.
say: Seed brings delta 4, alpha 1, Zeta -2, charlie 3, bravo 1, and a plain `target $Row #Row` yields exactly that spawn order.
`target $Row #Row by Row.rank as r` sorts when the rows are read, so -2 Zeta comes first. Ints sort numerically, and `by` comes before `as`.
`by Row.title` compares strings ordinally, so capital 'Zeta' comes before every lowercase name. The sort is stable: alpha and bravo both have rank 1 and keep spawn order.
`Entity` says which identity, and `Index` says which iteration, starting at 0. In entities_index.vein, `(Index + 1) + ". "` numbers six rows from 1 with no counter variable.
`if Index < 3` is a top-three cutoff, `Index % 2 == 0` stripes (0 alpha, 2 gamma, 4 epsilon), and `Index == 0` finds the first row.

`Index` counts position in the order the loop already yields. It never sorts. If you run `veinc run samples/entities_index.vein --ticks 1` after the main run, crop it after 'first is alpha': its last section prints three rows under '-- first two of the wide ones --' (see Watch out).

show.caption: Five rows, deliberately out of order
Spawn order, by rank, by title, and ties
Index: numbering, a cutoff, striping, the first row

gotchas: Ascending only, by one field. There is no descending order (SYNTAX-DECISIONS D13).

Strings compare ordinally, so capitals come first. `by` takes a `Shape.field`, not an expression, so there is no `by lower(Row.title)`. For a case-insensitive order, give the shape a field holding `lower(title)` and sort `by Row.thatField`. In a plain comparison, `lower(a) < lower(b)` and `lower(a) == lower(b)` already ignore case (RULES 14b, 28, 28e).

entities_index.vein's last block is stale: its label says 'first two of the wide ones' but it prints three rows, because the `if Index < 2` filter was removed. Keep it off screen, or relabel or restore it before filming.

`count` is lexed but unimplemented, so there is no built-in row count. To find the last row, count first (`var n = 0`, then `target $Row #Row as r { n = n + 1 }`) and test `Index == n - 1` in a second loop. The header comment calling the last row 'not expressible' is out of date (RULES 14c).
`Index` belongs to the nearest loop only (RULES 14c).
lessons.next: The templates so far took every argument. Real ones have a dozen fields, and you want to leave most of them alone.

lessons.title: Defaults, `base` and `?`
lessons.goal: Put defaults on shape fields, order includes so the optional fields trail, and use `base` and `?` at the call site.
lessons.hook: One argument builds a complete panel with seven fields, and the rule that allows it also decides how you lay out your shapes.
say: `builder Panel { $Content $Style $Layout   mark #Panel }` flattens to title, body, class, accent, padded, column, order. Include order is parameter order.
Only `title` has no default, so `bring Panel("Welcome")` is a complete call and prints 'Welcome' then '(no description yet)'.
There are no named arguments. To change `accent` you fill every slot before it, and `base` means 'the declared default here': `bring Panel("Danger", base, "panel warn", "#aa4444")`.
`base` fills a slot but does not skip it: `bring Panel("Footer", base, base, base, false, 1, 9)` still passes seven arguments, and its `order` of 9 is why Footer prints last.

The `"salu"` call is the output of `veinc scaffold samples/builder_defaults.vein '&Panel'` pasted in, with the REQUIRED title's `base` replaced by "salu". There is one slot per line, each labelled with its type, its shape and whether it's required, and a comma after every slot but the last.
`?` is the other tool: `bring Draft("Untitled", ?)` knowingly leaves `note` empty and still honours `slug`'s default. The output shows note=[] slug=[untitled].

show.caption: Three shapes with defaults, ordered so the optional fields trail
Five ways to call the same builder

show.anchor: shape $Draft { title: string, note: string, slug: string = "untitled" }
show.caption: `?`: leave a required field empty on purpose

gotchas: Only a TRAILING run of defaults is optional. A default in the middle is a required slot nothing can skip, and include order decides which is which (RULES 9). The on-screen comment undercounts: swapping `$Content` and `$Layout` puts `title` 6th, behind five defaults, and `bring Panel("Welcome")` then draws VS0230 ('column' is int) and VS0228 ('needs 6 argument(s)').
`base` on a parameter with no default is VS0231.
Leaving a required field out without `?` is VS0228, and `?` goes inside the parentheses (RULES 26).
`base` is a keyword only in expression position. It's still legal as a field name, and KEYWORDS.md doesn't list it.
The output heading says 'column/order', but only `order` drives the sort (the Show shard reads `by Layout.order`).
lessons.next: A default names the usual value for one field. What about naming a whole set of arguments, like 'a big coin is a coin worth five'?

lessons.title: Variants with `from`
lessons.goal: Derive a builder from another with `from`, fixing parameters by name and adding marks.
lessons.hook: A big coin is a coin worth five. Say that once, not at every call site.
say: Coin includes `$Position` and `$Prize`, so it takes five parameters (x, y, z, value, sound) and carries `mark #Coin`.
`builder BigCoin from Coin { value = 5 }` fixes `value` by name, so BigCoin takes four arguments.
`builder GoldCoin from BigCoin { sound = "gold.wav"   mark #Shiny }` chains: it inherits value = 5, fixes sound, and adds a mark, leaving three arguments.
All three carry #Coin, so Show finds all three (worth 1, 5 and 5), and Shine, which targets `$Prize #Shiny`, prints 'shiny coins: 1'.
Parameters are fixed by name, never by position, so a shape added to Coin reaches every variant.

show.anchor: shape $Position { x: float, y: float, z: float }
show.caption: A base builder and two variants, each taking fewer arguments
Variants inherit #Coin; only GoldCoin adds #Shiny

gotchas: An unknown base is VS0238 and a cycle is VS0239 (RULES 7c).
A fixed parameter consumes no argument. The remaining slots still bind in order (RULES 7c, 9).
A builder cannot call a builder, because its body is a signature, not statements. `from` is how you derive one.
Whole floats print without `.0`, so x=1.0 shows as 'x=1'.
lessons.next: That's templates done. Back to the tick loop, and to dice you can replay.

lessons.part: Deep dive: chance, motion and kits
lessons.title: `chance N%`, seeded and replayable
lessons.goal: Use `chance N%` blocks, know they draw from one generator seeded at 0, and step the same run frame by frame in the Workbench.
lessons.hook: Randomness you can replay: I'll run this twice, and you'll see exactly the same dice.
say: Seed makes four mobs by hand with `spawn()`, `attach $Health to e { hp: 20 }` and `mark e #Mob`, the long form a builder would shorten.
Rot gives each mob two draws per tick: `chance 50% { self.Health.hp -= 1 }` and `chance 25% { self.Health.hp -= 3 }`. `50%` is a real literal, not a string.
There is one generator, seeded at 0, so the same source and tick count print the same numbers every run. In this run e1 never loses hp and e4 is at 13 after four ticks.
Both chance blocks write the same `folds sum` field, and Report reads it in `settled`.

Live in the Workbench: the header line becomes the ▶ command box. Press ▶, then ↻, and get the same sixteen lines. Change it to `--ticks 40`: nothing checks for death, so every mob ends far below zero.
Then the Runtime panel: press Boot, Step ▸ four times, and type `hp` in the watch box. Every Boot starts a fresh interpreter with the same seed.

show.caption: Four mobs, two dice per tick, one seeded generator

gotchas: `#Mob` is never declared, so mark names go unchecked here: a typo like `#Mbo` would silently create a new mark (RULES 16).
Seeded means reproducible, not unpredictable. Don't use it where you need real randomness.
`random` is not a keyword, and `random()` is a built-in call. KEYWORDS.md still lists it as a keyword, which is stale.
Read the folded hp in `settled`, not mid-tick (RULES 13).
lessons.next: Dice were one kind of per-tick change. Next, per-tick change doing physics: two forces, one velocity.

lessons.part: Deep dive: chance, motion and kits
lessons.title: Two forces, one velocity
lessons.goal: Use stdlib shapes through qualified builder includes, watch a constant per-tick force build up into acceleration, and see the step lag one frame behind.
lessons.hook: Gravity and wind don't know about each other. Every frame both push the same velocity, one on y and one on x, and the object falls faster and faster along a straight slant.
say: Mover includes `*Vein.Transform.Spatial.$Position` and `*Vein.Transform.Spatial.$Velocity`: `bring Mover(0.0, 100.0, 0.0,  0.0, 0.0, 0.0)` gives position first, then velocity.
Ticker carries Vein.Time's `$Clock`, and `bring Ticker(0.0, 0.5)` sets `now` to 0 and `delta` to 0.5.

Gravity does `m.Velocity.y -= 4.9` and Wind does `m.Velocity.x += 1.0`. The stdlib declares every axis of `$Velocity` with `folds sum`, which is what lets two forces on the same axis both land. Here they push different axes, so each write would land even without folds.
Velocity keeps its value from tick to tick, so adding the same force every tick makes it grow, and a constant force becomes acceleration: v goes '1, -4.9', then '2, -9.8', then '3, -14.7'.
Step moves by velocity * 0.5, yet frame 1 prints 'at 0, 100'. Step reads the velocity as it stood at the end of the previous frame, which is an explicit Euler step.

The standard library ships shapes, not behaviour, so integrating position is the app's own Step shard. Live: step it in the Workbench Runtime panel and watch Position and Velocity change tick by tick.

show.caption: Stdlib shapes reached through qualified includes
Two forces on one velocity, one axis each, and the app's own step

gotchas: Read reconciled values in `settled`, and remember that folds accumulate rather than recompute (RULES 13, 13b).
The frame-1 lag is the phase boundary showing through (RULES 11, 12b).
The qualified `*…$Shape` form is for includes. `target` takes the bare `$Velocity` (RULES 17b).
Arguments bind positionally across includes even when field names collide (RULES 9).
Skip the header's 'NO CROSS-BUNDLE EVENTS HERE' reasoning. It's dated: clock_ticked.vein hears @Ticked and is in check-backend.
lessons.next: Here the app wrote its own Step shard. Next, a kit ships the moving shard for you, and one `need` line pulls it in.

lessons.part: Deep dive: chance, motion and kits
lessons.title: `need` a kit, get its behaviour
lessons.goal: Use an installed kit from bundles/ through one `need` line that both resolves its shared names and links its shards.
lessons.hook: The manifest names one file. A second bundle still runs, because one `need` line pulled it in.
say: `app KitDemo` loads only game.vein, and the banner says '2 bundle(s) linked into one runtime [KitDemo, Movement]; 1 of them by `need` [Movement]'.
`need "kit.Movement"` finds the kit by name under bundles/, makes its shared names usable bare, and links it.
The kit's public half is `publicator Drive`, with `$Mover` and `#Moving` each `shared`. `$Budget` sits outside the publicator, so no other bundle can name it.
The game's `builder Player` includes `$Position`, `$Mover` and `$Score` by bare name, plus `mark #Player   mark #Moving`.
The kit's `shard Drift` moves every `$Position $Mover #Moving` identity each tick, although the game never mentions Drift. The output steps 'at 1,0.5', 'at 2,1', 'at 3,1.5'.
Live in the Workbench: type `$` in game.vein. `$Mover` is offered, labelled with its kit, and `$Budget` is not.

show.caption: A one-line manifest
The kit: a public half, a private half, and a shard
The game uses the kit's shape and mark by bare name

gotchas: A leftover `*Vein.Console.Io.print("TEST")` in game.vein's Boot prints 'TEST'. Remove it before filming.

Movement.vein's comment on screen says the qualified form 'does not even parse' in a `target`. For this line that's right: `target $Position *kit.Movement.Drive.$Mover #Moving as m` is VS0100 "Expected 'as'". Only a lone `target *kit.Movement.Drive.$Mover as m` parses, and it then silently matches nothing. Either way, use the bare name (RULES 17b).
Shapes unify by bare name across bundles, so the kit's `$Position` and the game's are one component (RULES 15b).
`use Movement` is retired (VS0338): write `need "kit.Movement"` (RULES 18).
Only `shared("…")` inside a publicator crosses a bundle boundary (RULES 17).

lessons.title: A page by hand: fragments, a Kernel and a view
lessons.goal: Build the request → fragments → ShardView → response pipeline by hand, and see that declaration order is queue order.
lessons.hook: No function returns this web page. Two shards shout pieces of it, and a view stitches them together. Move one shard and the page goes blank.
say: `publicator SiteApi` declares the four events itself: `@Request`, `@Html`, `@Render` and `@Response`, each with a `shared("…")` label.
Header and Body both `hear @Request as req` and each emits its own `@Html { markup: … }` fragment. Nobody calls them.
Kernel also hears `@Request` and emits `@Render`. It's declared after the content shards, so its event queues behind their fragments.
`ShardView Page` keeps `var html: string`, appends every fragment with `html += f.markup`, and emits `@Response` with status 200 when `@Render` arrives.
`veinc render samples/site.vein /` fires one request with no socket. The trace shows Header, Body, Kernel, then Page, followed by `HTTP 200` and the page, and it names the event `@local.Site.Html`.
Live: move shard Kernel above Header and render again. You get HTTP 200 with `<html><body></body></html>`, because @Render was queued first.

show.caption: Content shards, a Kernel, and the ShardView that assembles them

gotchas: Under Git Bash set MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 for a `/` argument, or it becomes C:/Program Files/Git/ (RULES 23). site.vein never reads the path, so it still renders, but a routed site such as web_site.vein then prints '(no @Response emitted for C:/Program Files/Git/)'.
emit queues, and the queue drains only after every handler of the current event finishes. That's why Kernel's position matters (RULES 21).
An event's full name carries its bundle (RULES 20). Don't repeat the older 'events unify by bare name' wording from LANGUAGE-TOUR or STDLIB.md.
The `·` trace lines go to stderr, while the status and body go to stdout.
Don't use mypage.vein, shaped.vein or handles.vein for this idea: they currently render empty pages.

lessons.title: `audience`: who may be heard
lessons.goal: Make a shard carry shapes and marks, and gate a `hear` with `audience` so only matching emitters get through.
lessons.hook: Two shards send the same event. One listener hears only one of them, and the trace says it blocked the other.
say: `shard Combat $Session #Trusted { … }`: a shard can itself carry shapes and marks.
Sneaky carries nothing, and both shards emit @Damage on the same request: 5 from Combat, 99 from Sneaky.
`hear @Damage as d audience $Session #Trusted` fires only when the emitter carries all of the listed shapes and marks.
The trace says 'Shard.Auditor BLOCKS @local.Demo.Damage (audience) from Shard.Sneaky', and the body is 'audited trusted damage 5 from Shard.Combat'.
`d.from.kind` and `d.from.name` come for free, because every event knows who sent it.
The barrier belongs to the listener. Sneaky's emit succeeds, it just reaches nobody who will accept it.

show.caption: A trusted sender, an untrusted one, and a listener with an audience

`$Session` is never declared as a shape in this file, and it still compiles.
Set MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 under Git Bash for the `/` argument (RULES 23).
`veinc ir samples/events.vein` shows `carries=[$Session #Trusted]` and `audience=[$Session #Trusted]` if you want to show it on screen.

lessons.title: Behaviour as a component: rewiring every button
lessons.goal: Store behaviour as data on identities, replace it by re-attaching, and see the change land at the commit.
lessons.hook: Change what every button on a page does without naming a single button.
say: `fn fnName(e: Entity) return string { return "h" + e }` derives a function name from the identity, so nothing ever stores a name.
`builder Btn { $Element $Handler   mark #Button }`: a button carries its JavaScript body as a `$Handler` component, and Seed brings three.
Rewire walks every `#Button` and runs `attach $Handler to b { body: … }` again. Re-attaching replaces the component, and no button is named.
Before runs in the same `each tick` phase and still prints `console.log('one')` on tick 1, because the attach lands at the commit.
Show reads in `settled` and prints the `alert('one was rewired')` bodies. On tick 2, Before prints the alert bodies too.
The identity never changes, so `fnName` stays put: `h1`, `h2`, `h3` in every line. Only the body moves.

show.caption: Buttons as identities, carrying their handler
Rewire every button; before and after the commit

gotchas: `attach` is deferred to the commit point (RULES 11).
Inside one web request, wiring and rendering can't see each other, and `veinc serve` builds a fresh interpreter per request, so this demo runs on ticks (RULES 12b, 22).
Re-attaching a shape an identity already carries replaces it. There is no second copy.

lessons.title: A full site: pages rendered from a world
lessons.goal: Follow a site with four routes (/, /docs, /counter, /greet) where the cards, nav and buttons are identities, HTML, CSS and JS flow on three channels, and one view assembles them.
lessons.hook: The home page's cards aren't in the page code. They're identities, and the page is a query.
say: `SF navBar(path: string)` renders the nav inline: it targets every `$NavItem #Nav`, and the current page is bold rather than a link.
Home only contributes when `r.path == "/"`. It calls `navBar(r.path)` first, and because an SF runs inline its fragments land at the top.
`target $Card #Featured as self { bring Card(self.Card.title, self.Card.body) }`: the grid renders whatever identities the world holds, in spawn order. Open, OpenAs and Close each emit one fragment.

CounterSeed does `bring Readout("div", "count", "0") as out`, and each Btn's handler body is composed from `addNumber(domId(out), 2)`, `addNumber(domId(out), -2)` or `text(domId(out), "0")`, so no DOM id is typed by hand. It's dom_rewire's model: behaviour is a `$Handler` on the button.
ShardView Page keeps three accumulators, `html`, `css` and `js`, fed by `@Html`, `@Style` and `@Script`. It answers only if `html` isn't empty, and otherwise serve answers 404.
