lessons.title: One program, many windows: broadcast and roles
lessons.goal: Spawn named consoles, send to one, a random one or all of them on a timer, and give each window its own role with `match here()`.
lessons.hook: One command, four windows, and every two seconds the first one talks to the other three.
say: Opening a window is just an event: `emit *Vein.Console.Io.@Console { name: #Alpha, firsttext: … }`. The name is a mark, and it becomes that window's address.
`every 2 { … }` is a wall-clock timer, and `var n: int` is state that belongs to this shard and survives between rounds.
Each spawned window re-runs this same program, so `if here() == #Main` keeps the broadcasting in the window you launched.

Three ways to address: a fixed mark with `to: #Alpha`, a random one with `pick(consoles)`, and everybody with `target consoles as c` over a plain list. Inbox runs in every window and prints `m.from + ": " + m.text` for each line it receives. Only Alpha, Beta and Gamma are sent anything, so Main stays quiet after its opening line.
Live: run it and tile the windows. Every round Alpha gets its own line plus the broadcast, and one random window also gets 'you were picked'.
console_roles.vein generalises `if here()` into a role switch: Worker's `match here()` has Alpha echo to `#Main`, Gamma relay to `#Alpha`, and Beta count with `var seen: int`.

The `else` arm covers Main, which has no `when` of its own and prints the replies. Live: run `veinc run samples/console_roles.vein`, close Beta's window, and Main reports it as not running via `@Undelivered`.

show.caption: Opening windows is just emitting @Console
One, random, all, on a two-second timer
match here(): one program, a different job per window

gotchas: Without the `here() == #Main` guard every window would broadcast, since they all run the same `every 2` block.
Launcher's `run once` has no guard. Only the spawn itself is suppressed in a child, so each spawned window also prints the 'main — opening three consoles…' line.
console_roles.vein's Driver has a leftover `when #Alpha` test arm that sends 'FROM ALPHA TEST' to Beta every 2 seconds, and Worker's lines 78-82 are tab-indented. Clean both before filming.
Both headers mention `veinc build`, which writes an .exe. Use `veinc run` on camera.
There is no `!=`: the inverse guard is `not (here() == #Main)` (RULES 2). A match arm may start its own line (RULES 2b).
lessons.next: Windows on one machine talk over pipes. Next, a service that has never heard of VeinScript, over plain HTTP.

lessons.title: HTTP as a request and a reply
lessons.goal: Call an HTTP service with `@Fetch`, and handle `@Fetched` and `@Failed` separately.
lessons.hook: A web request with no await, no callback and no promise: one event goes out, one event comes back. And a 404 is not a failure here.
say: Boot emits `*Vein.Net.Http.@Fetch { url, method, body }` for httpbin's `/ip` once, and Poller emits another for `/uuid` every 5 seconds.
Results hears `@Fetched` and prints `r.status + " " + r.url`, then the body.
A 404 or 500 still arrives as `@Fetched`, because the server answered. `@Failed` means no answer at all (bad host, refused connection, timeout) and carries `f.reason`.
The request runs off the event loop and posts its result back, so `every 5` keeps firing while a slow host hangs.
Live: run it, watch the IP reply and then a fresh UUID every 5 seconds, and end with Ctrl+Z and Enter.

show.caption: Fetch once, poll on a timer, handle the reply and the silence

gotchas: The first reply is your public IP address from httpbin.org/ip: blur or crop that line in the edit.
It needs internet access to httpbin.org. Offline, every request arrives as @Failed.
`@Fetch` also has a `headers` field that this sample leaves out. A missing field reads as empty and is not warned about (RULES 26).
`var n` in Poller is incremented but never read.
To use a JSON body, parse it with `fromJson(r.body)` (RULES 24b).
lessons.next: HTTP asks a stranger. Peers are two Vein programs that know each other and prove who they are.

lessons.title: Peers: `@Listen`, `@Link` and a signed `audience`
lessons.goal: Connect two programs over TCP with a shared key, and filter whose messages are heard.
lessons.hook: The hub is never told where the spoke lives, and it still answers every ping.
say: The hub emits `*Vein.Net.Peer.@Listen { as: #Hub, at: 9700, key: "shared-secret" }`: `as` is who this program is on the network.
The spoke listens as `#Spoke` on 9701, then `@Link { name: #Hub, at: "127.0.0.1:9700", … }`. Linking registers a route and connects nothing.
Pinger sends `@Send { to: #Hub, text: "ping " + round }` every 2 seconds, the same shape as a console send.
Frames are signed with the key, so the hub's `hear … audience #Spoke` is a real barrier, not a request. Inbox, with no audience, still sees every message.
Trusted replies with `@Send { to: m.from, … }` to a peer it never linked. It learned the route from the signed frame.

Live: start the spoke first, and each ping comes back as @Undelivered. Then start the hub in a second terminal, and the spoke prints 'Hub replied: ack ping N'. A mark used as a value is its bare name, so there is no `#`.

show.caption: The hub: listen, a trusted handler, an inbox
The spoke: listen, link, ping

gotchas: net_peer's header says its `@Send` is 'byte for byte' the console version. The shape is the same, but the path is `*Vein.Net.Peer.@Send`, not `*Vein.Console.Io.@Send`.
`@Listen` refuses an empty key, and a wrong key looks like silence, because authentication happens at the receiver.
Ports 9700 and 9701 collide with the chat sample, so don't run them together.
Frames are encrypted under one static key. It isn't TLS: there is no forward secrecy and no certificate identity.
`audience` takes a bare mark (RULES 17b).
lessons.next: Put a roster of peers behind the hub and you have a chat server.

lessons.title: A networked chat in two files
lessons.goal: Run a TCP chat where the server keeps its roster as entities and relays each line to everyone except the sender.
lessons.hook: Laptop on the left, laptop on the right, one server, and not one line of socket code. The server doesn't know a single address in advance.
say: The server emits `*Vein.Net.Peer.@Listen { as: #Server, at: 9700, key: "chat-secret" }` once and never links a client.

The roster is made of entities: a newcomer becomes `spawn()` plus `attach $Client` with `addr: m.from`, and `target $Client` is how the server looks through it. `var known: bool` carries the answer out of the loop.
The relay skips the sender with `if not (self.Client.addr == m.from)`, because there is no `!=`.
On the client, `let first = not joined` snapshots the state. The first line you type is your name, and `@Listen { as: i.text, at: 0, … }` makes it your network identity, with the OS picking the port.
`@Link { name: #Server, at: ServerAddress(), … }` registers the route, sending "is here" puts you on the roster, and `audience #Server` on Incoming admits only the server's frames.
Live: start the server (it prints 'server listening on 9700'), then a client in each of two more terminals or machines. Type `bob` in one and `alice` in the other, then `hi bob`.
The server prints '* bob joined' and 'alice: hi bob'. Bob sees alice's lines, and alice never gets her own line back.

show.caption: The server: listen, keep a roster of entities, relay
The client: your first line is your identity
Only the server may be heard

gotchas: client.vein's `ServerAddress()` returns the placeholder "999.999.999.999:9700". Change it to "127.0.0.1:9700" (or the server machine's IP) before filming, or the client only reports that it can't reach the server.
The server machine must accept inbound TCP on 9700, and Windows may ask to allow it through the firewall the first time.
Every side must use the same key "chat-secret". A mismatched key shows up as silence, not as an error.
Several client.vein comments are stale (the address being typed in, alice.vein and bob.vein), so don't read them out.
`attach` is deferred (RULES 11), so the relay loop doesn't see the newcomer in the same handler. That's harmless, because the newcomer is the sender.
lessons.next: Every line in the chat was a string. The last part turns structured data and whole files into identities.

lessons.title: JSON in, identities, JSON out
lessons.goal: Parse JSON with `fromJson`, bring one identity per record in sorted order with `ordered by`, and serialise a shape back with `toJson`.
lessons.hook: A string arrives, becomes a world you can query, and each record goes back out as JSON with its types intact.
say: `fromJson(payload)` turns the string into plain data: objects become dictionaries and arrays become lists, so `doc.rows` is ordinary field access and `len(doc.rows)` prints 3.
The payload is four one-line string literals joined by `+`: each of the first three lines ends with a trailing `+`, which keeps the expression open (RULES 1, 3).

`target doc.rows as row: $Row` is an ascription: it declares what the outside data looks like, and fields are read directly as `row.title`. Today the compiler checks only that `$Row` exists (VS0233). A misspelt field such as `row.titel` still compiles and reads as empty.
`ordered by rank { … }` sorts the brings themselves. The payload arrived as 4, 1, -2, but the rows are spawned -2, 1, 4, so the plain query without `by` prints them in rank order.
`toJson(r.Row)` serialises the `$Row` shape on the identity in declaration order, for example {"title":"Zeta","rank":-2,"done":false}. Ints stay ints and bools stay bools.

show.caption: A JSON string becomes plain data
One bring per record, sorted as they are brought

show.anchor: emit *Vein.Console.Io.@Print { text: "-- as identities, in the order they were brought --" }
show.caption: A plain query in rank order, and back out as JSON

gotchas: `toJson` takes a shape (`r.Row`), never the entity, because nothing can ask an entity which shapes it carries (RULES 14, 24b).
Ascribed rows read `row.title`, while a component query reads `r.Row.title` (RULES 27).

This is interpreter-only: `veinc emit` still prints the C# (to stdout, or into a folder with `-o`), but it also prints a note for each of fromJson() and toJson() saying it has no C# emission, so this file will not compile (RULES 24b).
Malformed JSON parses to null, not a crash (RULES 24b).
`ordered by` reorders only `bring`, and every key is evaluated first (RULES 14d, 14e). The report is in `settled`, so run with `--ticks 1` or more.
lessons.next: JSON arrived as a string literal. Real data arrives from files, and a file is an event too.

lessons.title: Files are events: route them by tag
lessons.goal: Write and read files through events, tag each request, and route every reply through one checked `match f.tag`.
lessons.hook: Five files, one handler, and not one path spelled twice.
say: There's no open, close or handle: `@WriteFile` answers `@FileWritten`, `@ReadFile` answers `@FileLoaded`, and either one answers `@FileMissing` when it fails.
Seed writes five files, and each write carries a `tag`: `#Config`, `#Log`, and a computed `"slot" + (i + 1)` for three saves.
Ask hears every `@FileWritten` and reads the file back with `tag: w.tag`. The runtime hands the tag back untouched.
Route's `match f.tag` has `when #Config` and `when #Log` arms. A mark in value position evaluates to its own name, and `when` is checked against the declared marks.
Computed tags can't be named in a `when`, so the slots land in `else`: `bring Slot(slots, trim(f.text)) as s`, then `mark s #Save`.
The third slot emits `@SavesLoaded`, a new event, so the Report shard that hears it sees all three `#Save` identities. The output ends 'save 1: level=3' to 'save 3: level=9'.
`@FileMissing` carries the tag too, so its handler routes with its own `match m.tag` and the same `when #Config` / `when #Log` arms. The failure path needs no path comparisons either.

show.caption: Five writes, each tagged, three with computed tags
Read it back with the same tag
Success and failure, each routed by what the read was for

gotchas: Running it writes files under samples/out/ (gitignored). Paths resolve against the source file's folder, not the working directory.

The comment at line 42 says an undeclared mark is VS0210, and the header (line 30) and RULES 28c call a misspelled tag a compile error. The real diagnostic is VS0218, and it is a warning: a `when #Confg` typo prints 'warning VS0218: Mark #Confg is not declared in this bundle. known: #Config #Log #Save #Slot' and '0 error(s), 1 warning(s)', and `veinc run` still runs, printing 'untagged read: out/conf/app.conf' (RULES 16).
A `match` `else` may start its own line, but an `if`'s `} else {` may not (RULES 2b).
The report needs a separate event because brings commit per event (RULES 12b).
A failure is a message, not an exception (RULES 28b).
lessons.next: The saves became identities. Go further: turn every line and word of a document into an identity and ask it questions.

lessons.title: A text file becomes identities
lessons.goal: Turn a document's lines and words into marked identities, chain phases through events, and query them once they exist.
lessons.hook: `target $Line #Heading` is a sentence about a document.
say: The Parser walks `lines(f.text)`, which strips the line ending whichever it was, and captures `let number = Index + 1` because the inner loop rebinds `Index`.
Each line becomes an identity: `bring Line(number, line, len(words(line))) as e`.
A blank line gets `mark e #Blank`, and a line whose first word is exactly `#` gets `mark e #Heading`. The decision is made once and remembered as a mark.
Inside `target words(line) as w`, each word is brought as a `Word`. The mark goes on `e`, the line from the enclosing loop.
`emit @Parsed` ends the phase. Nothing brought above is committed yet, so the next event is where the identities exist.
The report's `target $Line #Heading as l` prints 'heading at line 1: # VeinScript' and 'heading at line 6: # Why identities', then '40 words; longest is 'identities.''.

show.caption: One pass over the lines; capture the line number

show.anchor: bring Line(number, line, len(words(line))) as e
show.caption: Lines and words become identities, and marks record decisions
A later phase asks the document a question

gotchas: Running it writes samples/sample-doc.txt and samples/sample-doc.report.txt next to the source file. Delete them after filming.
A `target $Line` in the same handler would match nothing (RULES 11, 12b).
`Index` belongs to the nearest loop (RULES 14c).
The comment at lines 141-143 says the language can't inspect characters. That's dated: `line[0]` and `chars()` work (RULES 28).
The header's `lines[i].startsWith("#")` is a contrast with method syntax VeinScript doesn't have. String functions are plain functions (RULES 28).

samples/demo.vein.title: Demo: the IOP core in one file
samples/demo.vein.summary: A compact tour of the core syntax: a shared $Health shape whose hp folds by sum, an @Damaged event, an SF, and a Drain shard that drains every #Enemy each tick, emits damage by chance, and marks the dead in settled. It never spawns anything, so it compiles and runs but prints nothing.
teaches: shape with a folds sum field
event with an included $Shape field and a var member
shard schedules: each tick and settled
prerequisites: the idea of a per-frame tick
samples/demo.vein.output:
`--- Shard Drain
     |--- EachTick
     |    `--- Target $Health #Enemy as self
     |         |--- Assign -= self.Health.hp
     |         |    `--- Int 1
     |         `--- Chance 30%
     |              `--- Emit @Damaged
     |                   |--- Arg amount = Int 5
     |                   `--- Arg victim = Ref self
     `--- Settled
          `--- Target $Health #Enemy as self
               `--- If
                    |--- Cond = Binary <=
                    |    |--- Path self.Health.hp
                    |    `--- Int 0
                    `--- Then
                         `--- Mark self #Dead
samples/demo.vein.notes: No run command in the header. `veinc run samples/demo.vein --ticks 3` exits 0 with no output (empty world). The output field holds an excerpt of `veinc ir samples/demo.vein` (the Shard Drain subtree), which matches the on-screen excerpt; the full IR is 33 lines. SF hurt is declared but never called (the header says so on purpose). docs/EXAMPLE-PIPELINE.md traces this file's emit through AST, HIR, IR and the backend.
talking_points: The schedule is the outer block and the query is the inner one: `each tick { target $Health #Enemy as self { … } }` visits every identity that carries the $Health shape AND wears the #Enemy mark.
`self.Health.hp -= 1` writes a field declared `hp: int folds sum`, so if several shards drain hp in the same tick their deltas add up instead of overwriting each other.
`chance 30% { … }` is a built-in probabilistic block, and `30%` is a real literal the lexer understands.
`settled` runs after the tick's fold contributions reconcile, which is why the `hp <= 0` death check lives there, and `mark self #Dead` tags the identity.
Three sigils, three kinds of thing: `$Health` is data, `#Enemy`/`#Dead` are tags, `@Damaged` is a message.
This file never calls spawn(), so the world is empty and `veinc run` prints nothing. `veinc ir samples/demo.vein` shows the compiled tree instead.
gotchas: RULES 10: the file has no spawn(), so every target matches nothing and `veinc run samples/demo.vein --ticks 3` prints nothing (exit 0). That looks exactly like a broken query.
RULES 13: reading hp during the tick sees an unreconciled value. Death checks belong in `settled`, as here.
RULES 11: `mark` is deferred to the commit point, after the folds.
RULES 16: #Enemy and #Dead are never declared. This bundle declares no marks, so mark names go unchecked and a misspelling would silently become a new mark.
RULES 15: $Health (a shape) and #Enemy (a mark) are different things with different sigils.

samples/payload.vein.title: Event payloads: defaults and auto-fill
samples/payload.vein.summary: Shows three ways a payload gets its values: a field default (@Hit amount = 1), auto-fill of an omitted field from the event being heard (a bridge re-emits @SyncedHit with no body), and plain dot access on the hear binding. The response reports where the event came from via the auto-tagged `from` origin.
teaches: emit with omitted fields (default or auto-fill from context)
hear ... as binding and plain field access
samples/payload.vein.output:
· Shard.Source [VF:Shard:Source#1] emits @local.Demo.Hit
  · Bridge.Sync [VF:Bridge:Sync#2] emits @local.Demo.SyncedHit
  · Shard.Report [VF:Shard:Report#3] emits @Response
HTTP 200
amount 1 from Bridge.Sync
samples/payload.vein.notes: The `·` trace lines go to stderr; HTTP 200 and the body go to stdout. The run used MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1. The file is in tools/check-backend.sh (payload.vein:2).
talking_points: `event @Hit { amount: int = 1 }` has a default, so `emit @Hit` with no body at all sends amount 1.
`@SyncedHit` has no default, yet the bridge writes `emit @SyncedHit` with no body. The missing `amount` is auto-filled by name from the event being heard, `h`.
Inside `hear @SyncedHit as s` you read the payload with a plain dot and no sigil: `s.amount`.
Every emit is auto-tagged with its origin: `s.from.kind + "." + s.from.name` prints `Bridge.Sync`, so the page says `amount 1 from Bridge.Sync`.

`veinc render` fires `@Request { path }` as the default boot event and prints the `@Response`. The `·` trace lines show each hop. The local events appear as `@local.Demo.Hit` because an event's full name is Author.Bundle.Name.
gotchas: RULES 23: under Git Bash, `veinc render samples/payload.vein /` needs MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 or the `/` becomes a Windows path and no @Response appears.
RULES 26: a missing emit field is not reported and would read as empty. Here it is filled by a default or from context, but outside those two cases an omitted field is silently blank.
RULES 20: local events are named Author.Bundle.Name (the trace shows @local.Demo.Hit), while runtime events like @Request/@Response keep bare names.
RULES 21: emit queues. Each hop runs after the previous handler finishes.

samples/events.vein.title: Audience: who may be heard
samples/events.vein.summary: Two shards emit @Damage on the same request: Combat carries $Session #Trusted and Sneaky carries nothing. The Auditor's `hear ... audience $Session #Trusted` lets Combat's event through and blocks Sneaky's, and the render trace logs the block.
teaches: First-Class objects carrying shapes and marks (shard X $Shape #Mark)
samples/events.vein.output:
· Shard.Combat [VF:Shard:Combat#1] emits @local.Demo.Damage
  · Shard.Sneaky [VF:Shard:Sneaky#2] emits @local.Demo.Damage
  · Shard.Auditor [VF:Shard:Auditor#3] emits @Response
  · Shard.Auditor BLOCKS @local.Demo.Damage (audience) from Shard.Sneaky
HTTP 200
audited trusted damage 5 from Shard.Combat
samples/events.vein.notes: Captured with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1. The `·` lines are stderr. Also ran `veinc ir samples/events.vein`, and it shows carries=[$Session #Trusted] on Combat and audience=[$Session #Trusted] on the Auditor's hear. In tools/check-backend.sh (events.vein:2).
talking_points: A shard is a First-Class object that can itself carry shapes and marks: `shard Combat $Session #Trusted { … }`.
`hear @Damage as d audience $Session #Trusted` only fires when the EMITTER carries all of the listed shapes and marks.

Both shards emit @Damage on the same request, and the trace says `Shard.Auditor BLOCKS @local.Demo.Damage (audience) from Shard.Sneaky`, so only `audited trusted damage 5 from Shard.Combat` comes back.
The barrier belongs to the listener, not the sender. Sneaky's emit succeeds and simply reaches nobody who will accept it.
`veinc ir samples/events.vein` shows the result: `Shard Combat  carries=[$Session #Trusted]` and `Hear @Damage as d  audience=[$Session #Trusted]`.
gotchas: RULES 23: pass MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 under Git Bash for the `/` route argument.
RULES 17b: audience takes a BARE $Shape/#Mark. A qualified one parses but resolves to nothing.
$Session is never declared as a shape in this file. The shard carries it by name only, and it still compiles.
RULES 21: emit queues, so the Auditor handles both @Damage events after the @Request handlers finish.

samples/functions.vein.title: fn computes, SF emits
samples/functions.vein.summary: Defines the two kinds of function, a value-returning `fn` (bonus, recursive fib) and an event-emitting `SF` (announce), then calls them locally and calls shared ones from other bundles through the qualified `*Vein.Math` / `*Vein.Console` paths.
teaches: fn with -> return type and return
SF as a named emit sequence (no return)
samples/functions.vein.output:
streak 3 bonus: 15
streak 99 bonus: 50
fib(10): 55
clamp(99, 0, 10) = 10
— all of the above came from four function calls
samples/functions.vein.notes: `bundle Functions by you` makes the author part of the bundle's name, so the shared fn is reachable as *you.Functions.Api.bonus(…). clamp prints `10`, not `10.0`.
talking_points: VeinScript splits functions by what they produce: an `SF` emits events and returns nothing, and a `fn` computes and returns a value.
`SF announce` is a named emit sequence. Calling it is a statement on its own line, and writing `-> T` or `return` in an SF is an error.
`fn fib(n: int) return int` recurses and is used in expression position: `announce("fib(10)", fib(10))` prints `fib(10): 55`.
`shared("…")` inside a `publicator` is the only thing that crosses a bundle boundary. A local fn like fib needs no `shared` to be callable here.
Cross-bundle calls use the qualified star path: `*Vein.Math.Scalars.clamp(99.0, 0.0, 10.0)` is a shared fn, and `*Vein.Console.Io.print(…)` is a shared SF.
`start @Boot { }` names the boot event, so `veinc run` fires @Boot first and the Scoreboard hears it.
gotchas: RULES 17: only shared("…") inside a publicator crosses a bundle boundary. Everything else is bundle-private.
RULES 17d: the shared("…") string is a short label and not a docblock. Over 160 characters is warning VS0243.
RULES 26: calling a fn/SF with the wrong number of arguments is VS0229, a warning and not an error.
RULES 21: an SF's emits queue. They do not print at the moment of the call.

samples/loops.vein.title: Four loops, break and continue
samples/loops.vein.summary: Runs VeinScript's four loops (while, repeat N as i, target over a list, target over identities) and cuts them short with break and continue: while uses both, a capped repeat uses break, and both target loops use continue. Players are brought in run once and reported in a separate each-tick schedule.
prerequisites: shards and schedules (run once, each tick)
samples/loops.vein.output:
while i=1
while i=3
while i=4
repeat r=0 Index=0
repeat r=1 Index=1
repeat r=2 Index=2
capped r=0
capped r=1
word 1 = alpha
word 2 = beta
word 3 = gamma
Ada scored 30
Grace scored 20
Ada scored 30
Grace scored 20
samples/loops.vein.notes: The Report shard runs every tick, so with --ticks 2 the two score lines print twice. With --ticks 1 they still print once, so the comment 'This is the second tick' means the phase after run once, not frame 2. RULES.md 28a says words() is interpreter-only, but CSharpBackend.IsPrebuilt now lists words, and this file is in check-backend (loops.vein:2), so that rule text looks stale.
talking_points: `continue` skips the rest of this pass and `break` leaves the loop. The while prints 1, 3, 4 because 2 is skipped and 5 stops it before it prints.
`repeat 3 as r` counts from 0, and `r` is the same number the built-in `Index` gives: `repeat r=0 Index=0`, and so on.
A count is a limit, not a promise: `break` at r == 2 stops `repeat 10` after `capped r=0`, `capped r=1`.
`words("alpha beta skip gamma")` returns a list, `target … as w` walks it, and `continue` skips the word "skip", so only three words are numbered.
The fourth loop is the identity loop, `target $Score #Player as p`, in the Report shard. It uses the same `continue`, which is why Alan (10 points) never prints.
The file is in tools/check-backend.sh because the interpreter once ignored break/continue while the compiled C# honoured them, and no sample used them.
gotchas: RULES 2: there is no `!=` or `!`. Conditions here use `==` and `<`, and inequality would be `not (a == b)`.
RULES 11/12b: `bring` commits at the phase boundary, so the Players brought in `run once` are queried from a separate `each tick` schedule, not in the same block.
RULES 14c: `Index` is the nearest loop's 0-based counter, the same number `as r` binds.
RULES 14b: the identity loop yields spawn order (Ada, Grace), which is the order of the brings.

samples/enum_state.vein.title: Enum state machine with match
samples/enum_state.vein.summary: A referee identity carries a $Match shape with an enum State { Kickoff, Play, Over }. Each tick advances the clock and the state by comparing enum cases, and a settled shard reads the state back with match, printing the phase every frame.
teaches: match / when / else on an enum field
samples/enum_state.vein.output:
t1 in play
t2 in play
t3 full time
t4 full time
samples/enum_state.vein.notes: In tools/check-backend.sh (enum_state.vein:4). This file supersedes the 'enum case does not work as a value' paragraph in samples/match_orders.vein.
talking_points: `enum State { Kickoff, Play, Over }` is declared inside the shape, and `state: State` types the field.
A case such as `State.Kickoff` evaluates to its own name, so it equals itself, differs from its siblings, prints, and can be matched.
Whistle runs in `each tick`: it bumps the clock, then advances the state by comparing cases, moving Kickoff to Play and then to Over once the clock reaches 3.
Commentary runs in `settled` and reads the state back with `match … when Kickoff / when Play / when Over`.

`builder Switch { $Switch   mark #Switch }`: in this one line the word refers to three of the four declarations and means something different each time.
`bring Switch(1)` spawns an identity, attaches $Switch with on = 1, and marks it #Switch.
Flip queries `target $Switch #Switch as s` and emits `@Switch { n: s.Switch.on }`, and Listen hears `@Switch as e` and reads `e.n`.
Look at the output order: `matched 2` prints before the two `@Switch says` lines. Report prints directly, while the @Switch path is one event hop further back in the queue.

gotchas: RULES 15: $Enemy and #Enemy are different things, and the same holds for all four Switch declarations.
RULES 7: the `mark` member is what makes the builder an identity template. Without it, bring would emit a fragment and spawn nothing.
RULES 11/12b: bring commits at the phase boundary, so the query lives in `settled` and not in the same `run once`.
RULES 21: emit queues. The @Print lines from Listen land after Report's @Print.

samples/bench_folds.vein.title: Benchmark: folds on the hot loop

folds sum reconciling two writers in one tick

`repeat 1000 { … }` needs no `as` when the counter is not used.
Drain subtracts 1 and Rot subtracts 2 from the same `hp` in the same tick. Because hp is `folds sum`, both deltas land instead of one overwriting the other.
It prints nothing on purpose: a @Print per entity per frame would be I/O and would swamp the number being measured, the cost of one activation.
The harness times two frame counts and subtracts them, which cancels process start and world construction.

RULES 13: two shards doing hp -= … in one tick combine because each contributes a delta from its own snapshot.
RULES 16: #Mob is never declared. The bundle declares no marks, so the name is unchecked.
RULES 10: spawn() is the only way to make an entity, and this file shows it without a builder.

each tick vs a clock event

samples/diagnostics.vein.title: No try/catch: failure is a message
samples/diagnostics.vein.summary: Shows what VeinScript has instead of try/catch: a Collector shard hears @DiagnosticRaised from anywhere in the program. Some diagnostics are raised on purpose with info/warn/error SFs, and one comes from a real runtime fault (`5 % 0`) that stops only its own block while the other shards carry on.
teaches: runtime faults become events; the block stops, the program lives
samples/diagnostics.vein.output:
-- checking the rows --
-- dividing --
   5 % 2 = 1
   note  | 2 rows to check
   WARN  | a row has an empty title
   ERROR | a row has rank -1, which is not a rank
   ERROR | Compute (once): Attempted to divide by zero.
-- the program is still alive --
   row: [write the docs] rank 3
   row: [] rank -1
samples/diagnostics.vein.notes: The header's 'Delete shard Collector below and the same six lines still appear' has the wrong count. With the Collector deleted (tested on a copy), FOUR diagnostics still print in the runtime's own format: `(info: 2 rows to check)`, `(warning: a row has an empty title)`, `(error: a row has rank -1, which is not a rank)` and `(error: Compute (once): Attempted to divide by zero.)`. They print inline, right after the line that raised them, instead of after the plain prints. The live edit works, but say 'four lines' and expect the order to change. The Unreachable shard hears *Vein.Net.Http.@Failed, which never fires here (no HTTP request), so it only illustrates the pattern. The row with an empty title and rank -1 is still brought and printed, because Validate reports but does not reject.
talking_points: There is no try/catch. The failure is a message: `hear *Vein.Diagnostics.Report.@DiagnosticRaised as d` is the catch.
A catch belongs to the code that failed, while a hear belongs to whoever cares. One Collector gets every diagnostic in the program without the failing shards knowing it exists.
`d.severity` is an int: 0 info, 1 warning, 2 error.
Validate calls `*Vein.Diagnostics.Report.info/warn/error(…)` when YOUR code decides something is wrong. Nothing failed, the program made a judgement.

The runtime raises the same event for a real fault: `5 % 0` in Compute gives `ERROR | Compute (once): Attempted to divide by zero.`. It names the shard and the phase, 'THIS LINE NEVER PRINTS' doesn't print, and Carry_on still runs.
The collected lines appear after the plain prints because the collector answers with another @Print, which joins the back of the same queue.
gotchas: RULES 21: emit queues, so the Collector's lines arrive one hop later than an inline @Print.
RULES 12b: Carry_on uses `settled`, not `run once`, because the rows brought in Validate's run once commit at the end of that phase. Another run once block would see nothing.
A fault stops the whole block, not just the statement: nothing after `5 % 0` in Compute runs.
An unheard diagnostic is never dropped. Without a Collector it prints in the runtime's own format.

samples/diagnostics_guard.vein.title: Guards: checking what arrived
samples/diagnostics_guard.vein.summary: Rows arrive as @RowArrived events, including one built from JSON with a misspelt key, and a Guard shard on that boundary rejects rows with no title (error), keeps suspicious ranks with a warning, and reports a total (info). It demonstrates that a static check catches what you wrote while a guard catches what arrived.
teaches: guard shard on a boundary event
choosing error vs warn vs info
missing values read as empty, not zero
samples/diagnostics_guard.vein.output:
-- four rows arrive --
   WARN  | row "ship it" has rank [0] — sent as 0, or the field name was misspelled and never arrived at all
   ERROR | row rejected: a row with no title cannot be shown
   WARN  | row "paint it" has rank [] — sent as 0, or the field name was misspelled and never arrived at all
   kept: rank   paint it
   kept: rank 0  ship it
   kept: rank 2  write the docs
   note  | 4 rows arrived, and these are the ones that were kept
samples/diagnostics_guard.vein.notes: Interpreter-only because of fromJson, and not in check-backend. The output shows '4 rows arrived' while only three rows are kept, because the empty-title row was rejected. The ordering of kept rows comes from `by Row.rank`, where the empty rank sorts first.
talking_points: The slogan of the file: a static check catches what you WROTE, and a guard catches what ARRIVED.
The guard sits on the boundary event `hear @RowArrived as r`, so every producer is checked without knowing the guard exists.
A missing string arrives EMPTY, not null, so `r.title == ""` catches both 'sent nothing' and 'sent an empty title'. That row is rejected with `error` and never brought.
The JSON row used the key `rnk`, so `rank` arrives empty. The output shows `rank []` next to the honest zero's `rank [0]`, and `r.rank < 1` catches both.

`warn` keeps the row. 'paint it' is brought with an empty rank and sorts first under `target $Row #Row by Row.rank`, and 'kept: rank   paint it' shows the hole. Moving the bring into an else would turn it into an error.
The final `note` prints after the kept lines because the collector answers with another event, one hop later in the queue.
gotchas: RULES 2b: `} else {` must be on one line. A newline after `}` orphans the else (VS0104).
RULES 1: the warn message wraps across lines with a TRAILING `+`. A leading `+` on the next line would start a new statement.
RULES 26: typing `rnk: 9` as a literal in an emit is VS0227. Only data from outside, like the fromJson string, gets past the compiler.
RULES 24b: fromJson is interpreter-only, and malformed input gives null rather than a crash.
RULES 12b: a bring inside a hear commits at the end of that event, so the report reads in `settled`.
RULES 27: `target rows as row: $Row` ascription is the static half for collection data, and it pairs with a guard rather than replacing one.

prerequisites: variables, loops and if in any language
the idea of a game loop that advances in ticks
entity + component idea (optional; this is the first identity sample)

enemy 2 hp 3

enemy 2 hp 1
enemy 3 hp 1

enemy 2 hp -1

`run once` builds the world: `repeat 3` runs spawn() to make an entity, attach gives it a $Health with hp 5, and mark tags it #Enemy.
Drain and Poison are two separate shards. Both run `self.Health.hp -= 1` on the same enemies in the same tick, and neither knows the other exists.

samples/console.vein.title: Console I/O as events
samples/console.vein.summary: The smallest interactive program. On boot it prints a prompt, and for every line typed at stdin it prints "you said <line>" back. It reads and writes the terminal only through stdlib events.
samples/console.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it waits for typed input. `bundle App` has no `by <author>` clause, unlike most newer samples.
talking_points: Everything lives in a `bundle`, and behaviour lives in a `shard`. A shard only reacts: each `hear` block runs when its event fires.
`start @Boot { }` names the entry event and `event @Boot { }` declares it. The runtime fires it once when the program starts.
There is no print function and no readLine. Emitting `*Vein.Console.Io.@Print` writes a line, and `*Vein.Console.Io.@Input` fires once for each line you type.
Read the qualified name left to right: `*` starts a path, Vein is the author, Console the bundle, Io the publicator, and `@` marks an event.
`as i` binds the event's payload, so `i.text` is the line that was typed. `+` joins strings.
The program runs until stdin ends: Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows, Ctrl+D on Unix.
gotchas: Rule 1: a newline ends a statement. If you wrap `"you said " + i.text` across lines, the `+` must end the first line, not start the second.
Piping empty input (e.g. `< /dev/null`) ends the run right after the prompt, because a root console run stops at stdin EOF.
The `@Boot` event has to be declared (`event @Boot { }`) as well as named in `start`. The two lines are not redundant.
Rule 20: stdlib and runtime events such as @Print keep one bare identity at runtime. The `*Vein.Console.Io.` path is written out so the reader can see where the event comes from.

samples/console_builder.vein.title: Spawning consoles with a builder
samples/console_builder.vein.summary: On boot it opens two new named console windows, #Server and #Client1, each printing its own first line. It does this by calling the stdlib Console builder with `bring`.
teaches: a builder with no output field emits @<BuilderName> (rule 5)
samples/console_builder.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it opens real console windows (second processes). It teaches the same thing as three_consoles.vein, which uses the emit form.
talking_points: Sigils tell you what a name is: `@` is an event, `$` a shape, `#` a mark and `&` a builder.
`bring *Vein.Console.Io.&Console(#Server, "Server ready.")` calls the standard library's Console builder. Arguments bind by position: a name, then a first line.
Console has no markup, css, code or line field and no mark. So bringing it emits an `@Console` event carrying its parameters, which is the same as `emit *Vein.Console.Io.@Console { … }`.
Console addresses are marks such as `#Server`, not strings. They are identities the runtime can route to.
Each new window is this same program relaunched under that name. It prints its first line and waits.
`by you` names the bundle's author. An event's full identity is Author.Bundle.Name.
gotchas: The header warns that a qualified `bring` resolves the stdlib builder at lower time. That works under `veinc run` and the Workbench, but a `veinc build` standalone exe cannot locate stdlib, so shipped exes should use `emit *Vein.Console.Io.@Console`.
Rule 5: a builder's output field decides what it makes. Console has none of markup/css/code/line/mark, so it emits @Console.
Rule 26: too many arguments to a `bring` is VS0204 (error). Too few is VS0228, a warning, and the missing parameters read empty.
Spawned windows re-run the whole program, and only the spawn itself is suppressed in a child. Anything else put in this @Boot handler would run in every window.

samples/console_broadcast.vein.title: Broadcast: one, random, all
samples/console_broadcast.vein.summary: Opens three console windows (#Alpha, #Beta, #Gamma). Every 2 seconds the launching window sends one message to Alpha only, one to a randomly picked console and one to all three. Every window prints what it receives, prefixed with the sender's name.
teaches: pick() random choice from a list
samples/console_broadcast.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run here because it opens three console windows (second processes). The launching window keeps broadcasting until its own input ends (Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows, Ctrl+D on Unix) or it is closed. Closing the three spawned windows does not stop it, and they exit by themselves when the launching window does. The header offers both `veinc build`, which writes console_broadcast.exe, and `veinc run`.
talking_points: `every 2 { … }` runs its block every two seconds of wall-clock time. `var n: int` belongs to this shard and keeps its value between runs.
There are three ways to address a message here: a fixed mark (`to: #Alpha`), a random one (`pick(consoles)`) and all of them (`target consoles as c` walks a plain list).
A spawned console re-runs this same program, so its timer fires too. `here()` is this window's own address, and `here() == #Main` limits broadcasting to the window you launched.
`#Main` is the reserved address of the root console, the one the user started.
The Inbox shard runs in every window. `@Message` carries `from` and `text`, and a mark joined into a string prints as its name.
gotchas: Without the `here() == #Main` guard every spawned window would broadcast too, because they all run the same `every 2` block.

The Launcher's `run once` has no guard. Only the spawn is suppressed in a child (ConsoleLauncher.Spawn returns when VEIN_CONSOLE is set), so each spawned window also prints the "main — opening three consoles…" line after its own first text.
Rule 2: there is no `!=`. `if here() == #Main` works, and the inverse is written `not (here() == #Main)`.
Rule 1: each `"round " + n + " — …"` concatenation stays on one line. Wrapping one needs a trailing `+`.

samples/console_chat.vein.summary: The launching window opens five named consoles: #Server and #Client1 to #Client4. A line typed in any window is sent to #Server, #Client4 and #Main, and every window prints what it receives as "<sender> says: <text>".
samples/console_chat.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it opens five console windows and needs typing. Most of it repeats three_consoles.vein (spawning) and console_broadcast.vein (send/receive).
talking_points: Launcher opens the windows by emitting the stdlib `@Console` event with a name mark and a first line. No builder is involved.
Chat is two handlers. A typed line (`@Input`) becomes `@Send` to three addresses, and a received line (`@Message`) is printed with `m.from`.
Every window runs the same file, so every window both forwards what you type and prints what arrives.
Each `@Send` crosses into another process. The header says the transport is a named pipe, but the program only names the destination mark.
`#Main` is the root window's reserved address, so a line can also be sent back to the launcher.
gotchas: The header says a typed line goes to Server and Client4, but line 35 also sends it to `#Main`.
Each spawned window re-runs the Launcher's `hear @Boot`. Spawning is suppressed in children, but the "Main — type here…" @Print still runs there, after the window's own first text.
The header's command is `veinc build`, which writes console_chat.exe. `veinc run samples/console_chat.vein` runs the program without building (console_broadcast.vein's header lists both forms).

when arms and an else arm
samples/console_roles.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it opens three console windows and runs on timers. The Driver's leftover `when #Alpha` test arm has been there since commit 8e6432a, and lines 78-82 use tab indentation; consider cleaning up both before recording.
talking_points: Every window runs every shard. What differs is `here()`, the window's own address, so `match here()` works as a role switch.
Alpha sends back to Main and Gamma forwards to Alpha, so a ping to Gamma reaches Main in two hops. Beta counts in `var seen` and reports the running total to Main.
The `else` arm catches any other address. Here that is #Main, which prints the replies.
`var seen` belongs to each process: every window has its own copy, and only Beta's ever changes.
The Reachability shard (lines 65-69) hears `@Undelivered` when a worker window has been closed. That is how the program tells a delivered message from one sent to nobody.
gotchas: Rule 2b: `} else {` must stay on one line in an `if`, but a `match` arm (`when`/`else`) may start its own line. This file is the example that rule cites.
Lines 78-82 (the `when #Beta` arm) are indented with tabs while the rest of the file uses spaces, so they look misaligned on screen in some editors.

The Driver shard has a `when #Alpha` arm that sends "FROM ALPHA TEST" to Beta every 2 seconds and declares unused `workers`/`dest` locals. It looks like a leftover experiment and does not match the header's role list ("#Alpha echoes").
control_center.vein explains that running this program twice pools the windows. Console pipe names are machine-global, so a send lands on whichever instance accepts first.

samples/three_consoles.vein.title: Three consoles from one program
samples/three_consoles.vein.summary: The simplest spawning demo. On boot the main window prints one line and opens three named console windows (#Server, #Client1, #Client2), each of which prints its own first line.
teaches: bare local names vs fully qualified stdlib names
samples/three_consoles.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run as a whole because it opens three console windows. Each spawned window re-runs the program and its `hear @Boot` fires again. The spawns are skipped in a child but the @Print is not, so every child window shows its own first line followed by "main — opening three consoles.". A simulated child (VEIN_CONSOLE and VEIN_CONSOLE_FIRST set) printed "Server console — ready." then that line. It teaches the same thing as console_builder.vein (builder form) and console_chat.vein's Launcher, and it is the smallest of the three.
talking_points: Spawning a console window is just an event: emit `*Vein.Console.Io.@Console` with a `name` mark and a `firsttext`.
Names written with the full `*Vein.Console.Io.` path come from the standard library. Bare names such as `@Boot` and `Launcher` are declared in this bundle.
Each new window is this same program relaunched under its own name. It prints its first text and waits.
A spawned console never spawns again, so the window tree cannot grow out of control.
gotchas: The header says a spawned console prints its firsttext and waits, but it also re-runs `hear @Boot`. The spawns are suppressed in a child and the "main — opening three consoles." @Print is not, so each child window shows that line too.
`veinc build` writes three_consoles.exe. Use `veinc run samples/three_consoles.vein` if you don't want an exe.
Rule 20: an event's identity is Author.Bundle.Name, and `by you` supplies the author part for this bundle's @Boot.

samples/control_center.vein.title: Control centre across three launches
samples/control_center.vein.summary: The same file is started in two or three terminals under different VEIN_CONSOLE names. Control keeps a roster of workers as entities and relays each worker's line to every other worker. Alpha and Beta never address each other.
teaches: VEIN_CONSOLE sets here() for independently launched processes
match here() role switch with else
relay to everyone except the sender
separate memory per process: only messages cross
samples/control_center.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it needs three terminals and typing. The terminal 2 and 3 commands are `VEIN_CONSOLE=Alpha veinc run samples/control_center.vein` and `VEIN_CONSOLE=Beta veinc run samples/control_center.vein`. The header includes a transcript of a real three-window run. The Relay handler is nearly identical to samples/chat/server.vein's, with console pipes where the chat uses the network.
talking_points: You start this one file three times. The VEIN_CONSOLE environment variable becomes `here()`, so `match here()` gives the Control process the relay role.
The roster is made of entities: one per worker, carrying a `$Worker` shape with its address. A shard `var` holds a single value, so entities are how this program keeps a growing list.
Looking someone up means walking `target $Worker as w`. The answer comes back in the shard's `known` flag, not as a return value.
A newcomer is added with `spawn()` followed by `attach $Worker to e { addr: m.from }`.
The relay sends to every worker except the sender. VeinScript has no `!=`, so that test is written `not (w.Worker.addr == m.from)`.
No memory is shared between the processes. Control's roster holds only what it has been told in messages.
gotchas: Rule 2: inequality is `not (a == b)`. There is no `!=` and no `!`.

Rules 11/12: `attach` is deferred to the commit, so the second `target $Worker` loop in the same handler does not see the worker that was just added. That is harmless, since that worker is the sender and the relay skips it anyway, and the next message sees it (rule 12b).
Rule 11: `destroy w` in Reachability is queued for the commit point, so destroying in the middle of the loop is safe.

The header says piping /dev/null into an instance ends it at once. That is only true of a run with no VEIN_CONSOLE (#Main). With VEIN_CONSOLE set, as in all three header commands, the process stays alive after stdin ends: Interp.Run only closes the loop when ConsoleLauncher.CurrentName is null. It keeps relaying, but nothing can be typed into it, so run each instance in a real terminal.

Setting the variable differs by shell: `VEIN_CONSOLE=Alpha veinc run …` in bash, `$env:VEIN_CONSOLE="Alpha"; .\veinc.cmd run …` in PowerShell, where the variable stays set for later commands in that session.
Console pipe names are machine-global, so a leftover instance on the same machine already listening as Control may receive the sends.

samples/chat.title: Networked chat: server and clients
samples/chat.summary: A TCP chat. server.vein listens on port 9700 as #Server, keeps its clients as entities and relays each line to everyone except the sender. client.vein asks for your name, uses it as your network identity and forwards what you type. alice.vein and bob.vein are the older version, one file per user with fixed identities and ports.
teaches: learning return routes from signed frames
samples/chat.notes: All four .vein files compile cleanly (`veinc check` prints ok). Not run because it needs a server and clients in separate terminals, network sockets and typing. As shipped, client.vein cannot reach a local server: ServerAddress() returns the placeholder "999.999.999.999:9700" (commit cbc8b96), so every send prints "(cannot reach 999.999.999.999:9700 — is the server running?)". Change it to "127.0.0.1:9700" before a local demo. The folder also holds client.exe (68 MB), which .gitignore excludes; it is left out of `files`. There is no vein.discovery file and no bundles/ subfolder. alice.vein and bob.vein are the same program apart from identity and port (9701 and 9702), and client.vein replaces them.
talking_points: The server emits `@Listen { as: #Server, at: 9700, key: "chat-secret" }` and never links a client. Each signed frame carries the port its sender listens on, so hearing from someone teaches the server how to reply.
The roster is made of entities. Joining is `spawn()` plus `attach $Client`, and leaving is `destroy` when a send to that client comes back `@Undelivered`.
There is no #Online mark on purpose. Existing is what makes a client a member, and a mark would be a second copy of that fact that could drift.
The relay skips the sender with `not (self.Client.addr == m.from)`.
client.vein uses the first line you type as your identity (`as: i.text`) and listens on `at: 0`, so the OS picks a free port. One file serves every user.
On the client, `audience #Server` admits only the server's messages. Frames are signed with the key, so that is enforced, not just requested.
gotchas: client.vein's ServerAddress() returns the placeholder "999.999.999.999:9700" (commit cbc8b96 replaced a real host). To demo locally, change it to "127.0.0.1:9700"; otherwise the client only reports that it cannot reach the server.

Several comments in client.vein are stale. Lines 18-19 say the server address is typed in, but it is hard-coded in ServerAddress(). Lines 13-15 say alice.vein and bob.vein 'used to' exist and that the language cannot read an environment variable, yet both files are still in the folder and VEIN_CONSOLE feeds here() (see control_center.vein). Lines 79-81 mention a `server` var that no longer exists.
bob.vein's header says the language cannot read an environment variable, while alice.vein's updated header says the opposite.
The fixed ports collide with other samples: the server's 9700 is also net_peer.vein's port, and alice's 9701 is also net_spoke.vein's. Don't run those pairs at the same time.
`@Listen` refuses an empty key, and every side must use the same "chat-secret". A mismatched key shows up as silence, not as an error.
`var` state belongs to one shard, which is why client.vein keeps its @Undelivered handler inside Session (the NOTE at the end of that file).

samples/net_fetch.vein.title: HTTP fetch: request and reply
samples/net_fetch.vein.summary: Asks httpbin.org for your IP once at startup, then fetches a fresh UUID every 5 seconds and prints each reply's status, URL and body. A request that gets no answer at all is reported separately as @Failed.
teaches: non-blocking I/O on the event loop
samples/net_fetch.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it needs the network (httpbin.org) and keeps polling until stdin ends.
talking_points: HTTP is a request with a reply. You emit `@Fetch` with a url, method and body, and later either `@Fetched` or `@Failed` arrives.
A 404 or a 500 still arrives as `@Fetched`, because the service answered. `@Failed` means no answer came back: bad host, refused connection or timeout.
The request runs on a worker thread and posts its result back, so `every 5` keeps firing while a slow host is still answering.
`r.status + " " + r.url` joins a number and a string into one line.
`@Failed` gets its own handler because a program that treats an unreachable host as an empty body will parse silence as data.
gotchas: It needs internet access to httpbin.org. Offline, every request arrives as @Failed.
Rule 26: `@Fetch` also has a `headers` field, which this sample leaves out. A missing emit field reads as empty and is deliberately not warned about.
`var n` in Poller is incremented but never read.
Rule 24b: to use a JSON body, parse it with `fromJson(r.body)`. This sample only prints the raw text.

samples/net_peer.vein.title: Network hub with an audience
samples/net_peer.vein.summary: The hub half of a two-program demo. It listens on port 9700 as #Hub with a shared-secret key, prints and acknowledges each ping from #Spoke, notes every message from anyone, and reports peers it cannot reach.
teaches: replying to a peer that was never linked
the same messaging vocabulary as consoles
samples/net_peer.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it listens on a TCP port and needs net_spoke.vein running in a second terminal. It is half of a pair; present it together with net_spoke.vein.
talking_points: `@Listen { as: #Hub, at: 9700, key: "shared-secret" }` sets who this program is on the network, the port it accepts on, and the secret that signs every frame.
`audience #Spoke` admits only frames proven to come from #Spoke. Because frames are signed, the barrier is enforced, not a convention.
The hub replies to `m.from` without ever calling `@Link` for the spoke. It learned the route from the signed frame.
Inbox has no audience, so it sees every message, including the spoke's. The barrier filters one handler and does not discard the message.
`@Send` and `@Message` are the same vocabulary the console samples use. Adding `@Listen` and `@Link` is what takes a program across machines.
gotchas: The key is mandatory. @Listen with an empty key is refused, because without it `audience` would mean nothing.
Rule 17b: `audience` takes a bare `#Spoke`, not a qualified path.
Each ping from #Spoke prints two lines, the 'trusted' one and '(inbox saw Spoke)', because both handlers hear it.

The header calls the sends 'byte for byte the console versions', but the source says `*Vein.Net.Peer.@Send`, not `*Vein.Console.Io.@Send`. They are the same runtime event (stdlib/Net.vein says so, and rule 20 keeps stdlib event names bare), but the text is not literally identical.
Port 9700 is also samples/chat/server.vein's port, so don't run both at once.
The header notes the encryption is AES-256-GCM under one static key. That gives no forward secrecy and no certificate identity, so it is not TLS.

samples/net_spoke.vein.title: Network spoke: link and ping
samples/net_spoke.vein.summary: The spoke half. It listens on 9701 as #Spoke, links #Hub at 127.0.0.1:9700, pings the hub every 2 seconds, prints the hub's replies and reports each ping that cannot be delivered.
teaches: every N timer with a shard var
only the address line knows about the network
samples/net_spoke.vein.notes: Compiles cleanly (`veinc ir` exit 0, no diagnostics). Not run because it needs net_peer.vein in a second terminal and the TCP ports. It is net_peer.vein's companion; show the two split-screen.
talking_points: `@Link { name: #Hub, at: "127.0.0.1:9700", key: … }` tells the runtime where #Hub lives. It connects nothing, and linking a machine that is not up yet is normal.
For two real machines you change only that `at:` address to the hub's IP.
The ping is a plain `@Send { to: #Hub }`. The routing table, not this line, decides that it goes over TCP.
`audience #Hub` on Replies accepts only the hub's signed answers.
The header suggests three steps: run the spoke with the hub down and watch @Undelivered, start the hub and watch the replies, then change the key and watch the hub drop everything.
gotchas: A wrong key does not fail at the sender. Authentication happens at the receiver, so a bad key looks exactly like a peer that went quiet.
Start net_peer.vein first, or every ping prints '(Hub is not up — …)' through @Undelivered.
Port 9701 is also samples/chat/alice.vein's listen port, so don't run them together.
Rule 1: `"ping " + round` stays on one line. Wrapping it needs a trailing `+`.

samples/app.title: Two authors, one bundle name
samples/app.summary: An app manifest loads two bundles that are both named Combat, one by yolan and one by alice, and both declare @Request. The author is part of every qualified name (*yolan.Combat.Api.@Request), and `veinc symbols` lists and flags the collision. The folder also holds RPGConsole.vein, a separate interactive console menu that app.vein does not load.
samples/app.output:
app MyGame  (197 symbols, 8 name collision(s))
  bundle Combat by alice
    *alice.Combat.Combat   (Bundle)   [COLLISION — qualify with author]
    *alice.Combat.Api.@Loot   (Event)
    *alice.Combat.Api.@Request   (Event)   [COLLISION — qualify with author]
  bundle Audio by Vein
  ... [truncated: the 16 Vein stdlib bundles, ~207 lines, including
       *Vein.Web.Http.@Request   (Event)   [COLLISION — qualify with author]] ...
  bundle Combat by yolan
    start @Request { path: string }   (boot — fill via `load … start { … }`)
    *yolan.Combat.Combat   (Bundle)   [COLLISION — qualify with author]
    *yolan.Combat.Api.@Request   (Event)   [COLLISION — qualify with author]
samples/app.notes: `veinc run samples/app/app.vein --ticks 1` printed only: "app MyGame: principal 'Combat' boots; 2 bundle(s) linked into one runtime [Combat, Combat]". The banner does not show authors, so both bundles appear as 'Combat'. RPGConsole.vein was not run because it is interactive (hear *Vein.Console.Io.@Input). It is a good optional demo of `target … by MenuItem.order` and menu-as-entities. The symbols output was truncated for length.
talking_points: `bundle Combat by yolan` makes the author the root of every qualified name, so this @Request is *yolan.Combat.Api.@Request.
Only what sits in a publicator with shared("…") is public. @Damage and $Health are bundle-level, so they are private, which is why `veinc symbols` does not list them.
yolan emits into alice's bundle with the full path *alice.Combat.Api.@Loot: author, bundle, publicator, member. No `need` line is required for a fully written path.
The manifest has no entry point. `load "yolan_combat.vein" start { path: "/mygame" }` overrides only the start field it names, and symbols prints that start signature so you know which fields exist.
`veinc symbols` marks both Combat bundles and both @Request events as COLLISION and says to qualify with the author.
gotchas: Running it (`veinc run samples/app/app.vein`) prints only the link banner, because no bundle emits @Print. This sample is for `veinc symbols`, not for runtime output.
RPGConsole.vein is in this folder but app.vein does not load it. It is a separate interactive program (bundle RpgMenu) that waits for typed input.
RPGConsole.vein's comment 'There is no string-to-number built-in' is out of date: int(x) and isNumber(s) exist (RULES 28d).

@Request is also a name the runtime raises itself, and Vein.Web.Http declares one too (RULES 20). symbols shows three @Request events, so the bare word is a confusing choice outside this collision demo.
Only shared("…") inside a publicator crosses a bundle boundary (RULES 17).
In RPGConsole's else-if chain, every `} else if … {` has to stay on one line (RULES 2b).

samples/app_capabilities.title: Apps: principal plus capabilities
samples/app_capabilities.summary: Three bundles are linked into one runtime. Store is the principal and its `start` is the app's only boot event. Billing (invoices shipments) and Audit (watches both) boot nothing and only react to events heard across bundles. Removing a `load` line removes that capability.
teaches: one shared event queue across bundles
samples/app_capabilities.output:
app Shop: principal 'Store' boots; 3 bundle(s) linked into one runtime [Store, Billing, Audit]
[Store] order: 3 x widget
[Audit] saw order of widget
[Billing] invoicing widget
[Audit] saw invoice 42 for widget
samples/app_capabilities.notes: The header command has no --ticks. It exited on its own (exit 0) and printed the output shown.
talking_points: The first `load` is the principal. Store's `start @Ordered { item: "widget", qty: 3 }` is the single event that boots the whole app.
Billing declares no `start`. It only hears *you.Store.Orders.@Shipped and emits its own shared @Invoiced.
Audit hears events from both other bundles without knowing how they are wired. Linking puts every loaded bundle on one queue.
Comment out a `load` line and that capability disappears, with no edit to any other file. That is the whole model.
Output order is queue order. '[Audit] saw order' prints before '[Billing] invoicing' because Audit's print was queued while @Ordered was being handled, ahead of the @Shipped work.
gotchas: Another bundle can only hear an event declared with shared("…") inside a publicator (RULES 17).
An event's identity is Author.Bundle.Name (RULES 20). Other bundles write *you.Store.Orders.@Ordered, while Store itself can say the bare @Ordered.
emit queues and does not run the handler immediately (RULES 21). Read the output as a queue, not a call stack.
There are no `need` lines: the full * path resolves the event, and the manifest's `load` is what links the bundles.

samples/app_net.title: The network as a capability
samples/app_net.summary: The principal Gate boots with a port number and never mentions networking. The capability bundle Wire hears Gate's @Opened, binds a real socket as #Hub with Vein.Net.Peer.@Listen, and acknowledges incoming messages. Because there is one _self per runtime, the whole app answers as #Hub.
teaches: one queue / one _self per app runtime
samples/app_net.notes: Not run: it needs a network socket and a second process. As a non-network check, `veinc symbols samples/app_net/hub.app.vein` loads cleanly (195 symbols; bundles Gate and Wire by you; Gate's start @Opened { at: int } is listed).
talking_points: Gate is the principal. `start @Opened { at: 9700 }` boots the app, and Gate says nothing about networks.
Wire's Listener hears *you.Gate.Doors.@Opened and emits *Vein.Net.Peer.@Listen { as: #Hub, at: o.at, key: … }, which binds a real socket.
There is one _self per runtime, so the name a capability claims (#Hub) is the name the whole app answers to.

Wire's Inbox is net_peer.vein's hub logic minus the barrier: it hears every *Vein.Net.Peer.@Message with no `audience`, prints it and sends back "ack …". In net_peer.vein the ack comes from the Trusted shard (`audience #Spoke`), and its Inbox only notes the sender. A hear works the same whichever bundle it lives in.
A send that cannot be delivered comes back as the @Undelivered message, not an exception.
Remove the Wire.vein load and the app is still valid, just local. Gate.vein does not change.
gotchas: You need two terminals: this app first, then `veinc run samples/net_spoke.vein`. The spoke's `hear … audience #Hub` only admits replies signed as #Hub.
The runtime refuses @Listen without a key (stdlib/Net.vein).
`as` is a keyword but is legal as a payload field name, as in `as: #Hub` (RULES 4).
Events share one queue across linked bundles (RULES 20), which is why a capability can bind the socket the app answers on.
Port 9700 must be free.

samples/bundle_collisions.title: Two kits, one word: @Dispatch
samples/bundle_collisions.summary: Two installed kits, acme.Radio and zenith.Courier, each export an event called @Dispatch with completely different payloads. One bundle needs both, emits each by its qualified name, and hears each with its own handler. Events are identified by Author.Bundle.Name, so both are deliverable.
teaches: shapes unify by bare name, events do not
samples/bundle_collisions.output:
app BundleCollisions: principal 'Collisions' boots; 3 bundle(s) linked into one runtime [Collisions, Radio, Courier]; 2 of them by `need` [Radio, Courier]
[radio]   news: broadcast to the channel
[courier] delivered to one person  urgent=true
samples/bundle_collisions.notes: The kits live in bundles/ and are found by name, not by path. Uncommenting line 43 in a scratch copy reproduces the header's VS0216 text word for word, but only where the bundle itself is compiled. `veinc check samples/bundle_collisions/collisions.vein` and `veinc run` of the app each print it three times with no line number (`:0:0`), while `veinc check` on bundle_collisions.app.vein prints 'ok'. It is only a warning: the program still runs, the ambiguous emit reaches neither handler, and the output is unchanged. Replacing the second need with `need "zenith.Courier" as C` (and writing *C.Post.@Dispatch) clears the warning, and the bare emit then goes to Radio: `[radio]   : which one am I?`.
talking_points: Two vendors who never met both picked @Dispatch. Radio's carries channel and text; Courier's carries to, text and urgent.
An event is Author.Bundle.Name, so *acme.Radio.Wire.@Dispatch and *zenith.Courier.Post.@Dispatch are two different events. Each hear reads fields the other does not have.
The manifest loads only collisions.vein. The banner shows the two kits linked 'by `need`' from bundles/.
A bare `emit @Dispatch` (uncomment line 43) gives VS0216, a warning about that one reference, and the fix is to qualify it.
The other fix is `need "zenith.Courier" as C`. An alias imports qualified and widens nothing, so the bare @Dispatch then means Radio's only.
Shapes still unify by bare name on purpose, so two disagreeing $Postbox declarations would still be VS0332.
gotchas: Events used to unify by bare name. Older notes may say two same-named events merge or fail with VS0332; that is no longer true for events (RULES 20).
`need` both resolves bare names and links the kit's shards (RULES 18). `need … as Y` widens nothing (RULES 18b).
Components still unify by bare name, and a shape cannot include a shape (RULES 15b).
This folder's own vein.discovery overrides samples/vein.discovery (the nearest file wins), which is why completion lists @Dispatch twice here.
`to: #Main` passes a mark as a value. Collisions declares no marks, so the name is not checked (RULES 16).

samples/kitdemo.title: A game built on an installed kit
samples/kitdemo.summary: A game bundle `need`s an installed kit (kit.Movement) that lives in bundles/. That one line lets the game use the kit's shared $Mover and #Moving by bare name, and it links the kit's Drift shard, which moves every #Moving entity each tick. A vein.discovery file shows that what the editor offers is a separate question from what is reachable.
teaches: shared public half vs private half
samples/kitdemo.output:
app KitDemo: principal 'KitDemo' boots; 2 bundle(s) linked into one runtime [KitDemo, Movement]; 1 of them by `need` [Movement]
TEST
at 1,0.5 after 1
at 2,1 after 2
at 3,1.5 after 3
samples/kitdemo.notes: Tested on a copy: `target *Vein.Transform.Spatial.$Position as m` compiled and matched 0 entities, while the bare `$Position` matched 1. Unlike motion.vein, the first frame moves here, because $Mover's rate is set once at spawn and already committed when tick 1 runs. motion.vein's velocity starts at 0, and each force's write only becomes readable the next frame. Folding is not the difference: a copy of motion.vein with an unfolded velocity shape shows the same one-frame lag.
talking_points: The manifest is one line: `load "game.vein"`. The game's `need "kit.Movement"` pulls in the kit, and its Drift shard runs even though the manifest never names it.
The kit's public half is `publicator Drive`: $Mover and #Moving, each with shared("…"). $Budget sits outside the publicator, so no other bundle can see it.
The game's builder Player includes $Position, $Mover and $Score by bare name. `bring Player(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0)` binds x y z, then dx dy, then points.
Drift adds dx/dy to $Position every tick, and the game's Watch shard reports in `settled`, so the output steps by (1, 0.5) each frame.
vein.discovery decides what completion offers and `shared` decides what is reachable. Delete `expose kit.Movement` and $Mover disappears from the `$` list, but the game still runs.
gotchas: The 'TEST' line in the output comes from a leftover `*Vein.Console.Io.print("TEST")` in Boot. Commit cbc8b96 says it was left in deliberately, along with loose whitespace in Watch. Clean both before filming.
Movement.vein's header says `$Internals` does not appear, but the private shape is actually named `$Budget`, so the comment is out of date.

`target` takes bare shapes (RULES 17b). Movement.vein says the qualified form 'does not even parse' there, and that is true for Drift's own line: `target *Vein.Transform.Spatial.$Position $Mover #Moving as m` is VS0100 "Expected 'as', found ShapeRef 'Mover'". A qualified shape on its own (`target *Vein.Transform.Spatial.$Position as m`) does parse, and silently matches nothing.
`need` links the kit's shards, not just its names (RULES 18).
The kit's $Position and the game's $Position are one component because shapes unify by bare name (RULES 15b).
Arguments bind positionally across includes, in declaration order (RULES 9).
In vein.discovery the most specific path wins, not the line order: `silent Vein.Transform.Motion` beats `expose Vein.Transform`.

samples/vein.discovery.title: vein.discovery: what completion offers
samples/vein.discovery.summary: A plain-text policy file, not a program. It controls what the editor's `*`/sigil completion lists for everything under samples/: `silent all`, then only Vein.Console and Vein.Math exposed, with commented examples of per-publicator and transitive rules.
samples/vein.discovery.notes: A config file, so nothing to run. samples/kitdemo/vein.discovery is a better on-screen version of the same idea: it demonstrates most-specific-wins and explains shared vs discovery. Parser: src/Vein.Compiler/Project/DiscoveryPolicy.cs.
talking_points: `shared` decides what can be used across bundles. This file only decides what is offered when you type a sigil.
`silent all` starts from nothing, then `expose Vein.Console` and `expose Vein.Math` add back two stdlib bundles.
A path is Author, Author.Bundle or Author.Bundle.Publicator. The most specific rule wins, whatever order the lines are in.
The nearest vein.discovery wins, so samples/kitdemo and samples/bundle_collisions have their own that override this one.

teaches: folds sum declared per axis on stdlib $Velocity (unused here: the forces write different axes)
velocity persists across ticks, so a constant push becomes acceleration
phase boundary: each tick vs settled
samples/motion.vein.notes: Listed in tools/check-backend.sh (motion.vein:4). Two header claims are out of step with the code. Lines 64-66 say Gravity and Wind write the same field, but Gravity writes Velocity.y and Wind writes Velocity.x, so `folds sum` never reconciles anything here. A scratch copy using an unfolded `shape $Vel { x: float, y: float, z: float }` printed exactly the same four frames. The fold only matters when both shards write one axis: with Wind changed to `m.Velocity.y -= 1.0`, v.y goes -5.9, -11.8, -17.7 with the stdlib fold and -1, -2, -3 without it, because the last write wins. The 'NO CROSS-BUNDLE EVENTS HERE' paragraph (lines 21-27) is also dated: stdlib_events.vein and clock_ticked.vein, which hears @Ticked, are both in check-backend.sh now.
talking_points: `bring Mover(0.0, 100.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)`: the first three arguments fill the qualified $Position include and the next three fill $Velocity.

Gravity writes Velocity.y and Wind writes Velocity.x in the same frame, and neither knows about the other. Because they touch different axes, both land even without a fold. `folds sum` on stdlib's $Velocity is what lets two shards push the SAME axis: change Wind to `m.Velocity.y -= 1.0` and v.y drops 5.9 per tick with the fold, but only 1 per tick without it, because the last write wins.

Velocity is stored state and each tick adds to it, so a constant -4.9 per tick becomes acceleration: v.y goes -4.9, -9.8, -14.7, -19.6. That comes from `-=` on a persistent field, not from the fold. An unfolded copy accumulates the same way.
The first frame does not move (at 0, 100). Step reads velocity as it stood at the end of the previous frame, which is an explicit Euler step.
Report runs in `settled`, after reconciliation, and rounds with *Vein.Math.Round.roundTo.
The standard library is vocabulary, not a framework: it declares no shards, so the integration step belongs to the app.
gotchas: folds reconciles concurrent writes, and the reconciled value is read in `settled` (RULES 13). folds accumulates and does not recompute (RULES 13b).

Every write made during `each tick`, folded or not, becomes readable only once the phase commits (RULES 13). Step therefore reads the velocity as it stood before this frame's forces, which is the frame-1 lag. An unfolded copy of the velocity shape lags the same way.
Report's multi-line `text:` works only because each line ends with `+` (RULES 1).
Arguments bind positionally across includes (RULES 9).
The header's 'NO CROSS-BUNDLE EVENTS HERE' reasoning looks out of date: stdlib_events.vein and clock_ticked.vein (which hears @Ticked) are now in tools/check-backend.sh.

total functions: indexOf answers -1, substring clamps, nothing throws
walking a list with target lines(...) as line

talking_points: indexOf gives the position, or -1 when the text isn't there (see 'missing = -1'), so indexOf(s, x) >= 0 means 'is it in there' with no second call.
substring comes in two forms, start-to-end or start plus length. Here we find the colon and cut 'ERROR' in front of it and 'disk full on /dev/sda1' after it (colon + 2).

These functions never throw. substring past the end gives an empty string, and asking for 99 characters of "abc" from index 1 just gives "bc". VeinScript has no catch, so the operations don't need a guard.

collection target with a type ascription (as row: $Row)
ordered by sorts the brings, so spawn order becomes rank order
toJson takes a shape on an identity, not the identity

`as row: $Row` is an ascription: it says what the outside records look like and types row.title for the tooling. It does not catch a misspelt field today. It describes a record, so you read row.title, not row.Row.title (RULES 27).

That's why the first query in Report has no `by` and still prints in rank order: query order is spawn order (RULES 14b, 14e).

It flips one setting in the config with replace (writing only when something changed) and scans the log for ERROR/FATAL lines, turning each into a $Problem identity with a #Fatal mark where it applies.
teaches: idempotent edit guard to break a write -> re-read -> write loop
filtering lines with contains/startsWith and `and not`
bring ... as e plus mark to remember a decision
routing by f.path (and why it stops scaling)
prerequisites: target over a list and over identities

log: 2 line(s) worth keeping
  line 2: ERROR disk full
  line 4: FATAL out of memory

samples/file_edit.vein.notes: Running it writes samples/config.txt and samples/server.log next to the source whatever the working directory, because relative paths resolve against the .vein file's folder. Neither file is gitignored, so delete them after a demo. There is a possible logic slip in shard Scan: a line that starts with FATAL and also contains ERROR would be brought twice, once per `if`. The sample data has no such line, so the output is unaffected.
talking_points: There's no open or close. A file is an event: we emit @ReadFile and hear @FileLoaded, the same request-and-answer shape as @Fetch/@Fetched.
The whole edit is one replace call: replace(f.text, "fullscreen = false", "fullscreen = true").
The guard `if not (updated == f.text)` is what matters. A write answers @FileWritten, the Verify shard reads the file again, and without the guard Config would edit and write forever.
On the second pass there's nothing left to replace, so updated equals the text that was read and the cycle stops. The output prints 'config: fullscreen switched on' exactly once.
Inequality has no != here, so 'it changed' is written `not (updated == f.text)`.

The Scan shard shows the other job: target lines(f.text), keep lines that contain ERROR but not 'test', bring Problem(Index + 1, l) as e, and mark FATAL ones. The report then queries #Fatal without repeating the test.

There's no != or !, so write not (a == b) (RULES 2).
Routing with `if f.path == "..."` fails silently on a typo and doesn't scale. file_tags.vein routes by tag instead (RULES 28c).
Relative paths resolve against the .vein file's own folder (Interp.BaseDirectory = the source directory), not the working directory. Running this creates samples/config.txt and samples/server.log.

In Scan, a line that both starts with FATAL and contains ERROR would be brought twice: once in the ERROR branch (which also marks it #Fatal) and again in the separate startsWith(l, "FATAL") block. The sample data has no such line, so the output is unaffected.
The attach and mark from bring are deferred to the event's commit, which is why the report runs on a separate @Scanned event (RULES 11, 12b).
