samples/file_tags.vein.summary: Writes five files (a config, a log and three computed save slots), each carrying a tag. One @FileLoaded handler routes on `match f.tag` instead of comparing paths. Save slots with computed tags land in the else arm, become #Save identities and are reported once all three are in.
teaches: the tag field on file events, echoed back untouched
a mark in value position evaluates to its own name
match / when / else checked against declared marks
the failure path (@FileMissing) routes through the same match

save 2: level=6
save 3: level=9

talking_points: @FileLoaded fires for every file the program reads. Instead of a wall of `if f.path == ...`, this one handler does `match f.tag`.
The tag is set when the file is requested (tag: #Config) and the runtime hands it back unchanged. A mark in value position is just its own name, so both ends are the same string with no quotes.

`when` is checked against declared marks, so misspelling #Config is flagged: `when #Confg` gives warning VS0218 'Mark #Confg is not declared in this bundle. known: #Config #Log #Save #Slot'. It is a warning, not an error, so the program still builds and runs. The #Config arm never matches, and the config read falls through to `else`, which prints 'untagged read: out/conf/app.conf' instead of 'config: fullscreen = false'.
The tag field is a string, so it can be computed. Seed writes "slot" + (i + 1) inside `repeat 3`. No `when` can name those, so they fall into else and are matched with startsWith(f.tag, "slot").
The Ask shard never spells a path. It passes w.path and w.tag from @FileWritten straight into @ReadFile, so a file that moves changes only in Seed.
Failures route the same way: @FileMissing carries the tag too and goes through its own match. Output ends with save 1..3 at level 3, 6 and 9.

A match `else` may start its own line (RULES 2b), but an if's `} else {` must stay on one line, and this excerpt has both.
Computed tags can't appear in a `when`; handle them in the else arm.
repeat 3 as i counts from 0, hence the (i + 1) for slot1..slot3.
Relative paths resolve against the .vein file's folder, so this run writes samples/out/conf/app.conf, samples/out/logs/server.log and samples/out/saves/slot1-3.dat.
The report is triggered by @SavesLoaded, a separate event, because the brings in Route aren't committed until that handler's event ends (RULES 12b).

marking a decision once instead of re-testing it

Index in nested loops; capture the outer one in a let
query order == bring order; Entity ids

target queries by shape and mark

A blank line isn't thrown away. It becomes an identity marked #Blank, so 'how many blank lines?' is a query later.

`as` only works on an identity template, meaning a builder with a mark member. On a fragment builder it's VS0221 (RULES 7, 7b).
The Loader checks w.path == "sample-doc.txt"; without that it would read back its own report and parse it as the document.
Relative paths resolve against the .vein file's folder, so running this creates samples/sample-doc.txt and samples/sample-doc.report.txt.
Entity ids have gaps (e1, e4, e5 ...) because words take ids between lines. They appear in the written report file, not in the console output.

samples/db_query.vein.title: PostgREST queries against Supabase
samples/db_query.vein.summary: Builds six Supabase/PostgREST query URLs (basic select, filters, set membership, OR, paging, and an embedded join), fires them all at once through the stdlib *Vein.Rest.Db.get, and prints the rows from each reply. The joined query's nested comments are walked with a nested target.
teaches: a REST call is emit @Fetch / hear @Fetched (via the stdlib SF Db.get)
announcing a connection once with bring *Vein.Rest.Db.&Connect
telling concurrent replies apart by f.url
4xx/5xx arrive on @Fetched; @Failed means no answer at all
fromJson lists and a nested target over row.comments
samples/db_query.vein.notes: Not run: needs a network and real Supabase credentials, and `veinc run` keeps pumping stdin until EOF. Stdlib verified: stdlib/Rest.vein defines builder Connect { $Connection } (emits @Connect), SF get(root, key, path) and Status.ok/clientError. The SF parameter is named `root` because `base` is a keyword in expression position.
talking_points: Each query is just a URL built by an ordinary fn. qEmbed nests a related table inside select as comments(id,body), and the foreign key does the join, so there's no `on` clause.
Boot declares the connection once: `bring *Vein.Rest.Db.&Connect(site(), key())` emits @Connect, and any shard that cares hears it and reads c.base and c.key.
The Queries shard fires six *Vein.Rest.Db.get calls at once. get is a stdlib SF that emits @Fetch with the paired apikey and Bearer headers.
The replies come back in whatever order the service answers, so every @Fetched carries the url that caused it. That's what embedUrl() is for later.
Elsewhere in the file, a 4xx/5xx still arrives on @Fetched (checked with *Vein.Rest.Status.ok), while @Failed means nothing replied at all.
The filter syntax is column=operator.value joined with &, e.g. rank=gte.3, rank=in.(1,3), or=(rank.eq.1,done.is.true), plus limit/offset, which always need an order.
gotchas: It needs a real Supabase project URL and anon key in site()/key() and two tables (tasks, comments). With the placeholders there's nothing to show.
VeinScript has no percent-encoding, so only interpolate values you control and filter user input in an `if` inside the target loop.
Check Status.ok(f.status) before fromJson. An error body parses fine and gives you the wrong rows.
Two shards both hear @Fetched, and each must filter on f.url or they'll both handle every reply.
@Fetched carries only url, status and body, so a Content-Range total (Prefer: count=exact) can't be read.
Interpreter-only: emit/hear is skipped by the C# backend. Coverage is NetHttpTests, not check-backend.

samples/db_supabase.vein.title: Supabase read and write
samples/db_supabase.vein.summary: Holds Supabase credentials as a $Connection identity, GETs a tasks table, and turns each returned row into a $Task identity. It then lists the tasks by rank and POSTs a new $Draft row serialised with toJson. All of it is @Fetch/@Fetched events; there's no database driver.
teaches: credentials as an identity (&Connection) versus an announcement event (&Connect)
fromJson list plus ascription `target rows as row: $Task`
emit a follow-up event (@Loaded) because brings are not yet committed
an event that includes a stdlib shape (*Vein.Rest.Db.$Connection)
a separate $Draft shape for rows without a server-assigned id
toJson(d.Draft) for a POST body; Status.ok / clientError
samples/db_supabase.vein.notes: Not run: needs a network and a real Supabase project, and `veinc run` pumps stdin. The comment at lines 101-103 contradicts the current RULES.md 12c (nested target bindings are now both readable), so the stated reason for carrying credentials on @Loaded is outdated, though the design still works. Line 217 ('VeinScript cannot find a character to escape') is also dated given RULES 28 (s[0], chars()).
talking_points: This code sits inside `target $Connection #Connection as c`. The credentials are an identity brought in Boot, so any shard can look them up instead of having them passed in.
@Fetched fires for every request, so we compare f.url with the select URL to tell the SELECT's reply from the POST's.
PostgREST answers a select with a bare JSON array, and fromJson returns it as a list that len measures and target walks.
`target rows as row: $Task` says what the outside data looks like. Fields are read directly as row.title, and each row becomes a $Task identity through bring Task(...).
Those brings aren't committed yet, so instead of listing them here it emits @Loaded carrying the count and the connection. The Listing and Write shards react to that.
The else branch is the reply to the insert, where Write POSTed `[` + toJson(d.Draft) + `]`. $Draft has no id because Postgres assigns it.
gotchas: The URL and key are placeholders. An anon key is only safe with row-level security on, and the service_role key must never be committed.

`veinc run` keeps pumping stdin until EOF, and --ticks doesn't help because ticks run back to back and never wait for a network reply. That's also why the kickoff is an event, not `settled`, per the file's comments.
A 401/404/500 arrives on @Fetched, not @Failed. Without the Status.ok check, fromJson gets an error object and you get zero rows.
Brings in a hear are invisible until that event commits, so query them from a later event such as @Loaded (RULES 12b).
Reusing $Task for the insert would make toJson post "id": 0. The id-less $Draft shape exists to prevent that.
Stale comment at lines 101-103 says a nested target 'silently reads the OUTER binding as empty (docs/RULES.md 12c)'. RULES 12c now says nested targets bind by name and both bindings are readable.

excluded.samples/LANGUAGE-TOUR.vein: a hand-made digest of the older samples. Its code is in the samples themselves, and some of its comments are stale (they still teach `use` and bare-name events).
excluded.samples/web_app/shards/Reference.vein: the `/docs` route of web_app, generated by tools/gen-reference.js from the reference HTML. It is 2,579 lines of documentation text, not teaching code.

glossary.meaning: The paradigm. A program is a set of identities that carry data and tags. All behaviour lives in shards, which target matching identities. There is no class, and shards never call each other.

Something in the world: an id that shapes and marks hang off. `Entity` is also a keyword. As a type it is an entity id. As an expression it is the id of the nearest target binding, or 0 outside a target.
A built-in call, not a keyword. It creates an identity immediately and is the only way to make one. With no spawn the world is empty and every target matches nothing.
A named group of fields an identity carries (a component). Across bundles, shapes with the same bare name are the same component. A shape can declare an enum and can bring marks with it.

A tag with no fields that an identity wears. Declaring any mark at bundle level turns on VS0218 checking for that bundle. Used as a value, a mark evaluates to its own name, which is how console addresses and file tags work.
A message type. A field with `=` is optional and one without is required. Since the last commits, an event's identity is Author.Bundle.Name, while a shape's is just its name.
Queues an event. It does not deliver right away. Omitted fields are filled from defaults, then from context (the event being heard, then locals).
A handler block. The binding reads payload fields directly, with no sigil.
Fields the runtime attaches to every event: id, from, origin, source, bundle, cause, trail. You never declare them. `veinc events` prints them.
A barrier on a handler: it fires only when the emitter carries every listed shape and mark. It is enforced over Vein.Net (signed frames) and only advisory over the local console pipe.
The only place behaviour lives: a set of schedule and hear blocks. A shard can never be shared or put inside a publicator (VS0108).

Loops over every identity that carries ALL the listed shapes and marks. Fields are read as binding.Shape.field. At least one shape is required (VS0236). Results come in spawn order unless a `by` clause sorts them.

glossary.syntax: target words(s) as w { … }  ·  target rows as row: $Task { … }
glossary.meaning: The same verb iterates any list. There is no for/in. An optional `: $Shape` ascription declares what outside data (JSON, DB rows) looks like, so its fields are checked.
A schedule that runs once at start. This is where worlds are seeded. `run` and `once` are contextual words, not keywords.
A schedule that runs every simulation tick. The clock is explicit: `veinc run … --ticks N`.
Runs after the tick's fold contributions are reconciled. This is the only correct place to read final values, such as death checks.
A wall-clock timer, in seconds.
A field modifier that says how writes from several shards in one tick combine: sum, min, max, replace, first, all, any. It accumulates across ticks and does not recompute.

glossary.syntax: attach $Health to e { hp: 5 }  ·  unattach $Health from e
glossary.meaning: Adds or removes a component. The change is deferred to the commit point, so it is invisible inside the event that made it and visible from the next one.
Removes an identity. The removal is deferred like the other structural changes.
The nearest loop's 0-based iteration counter, in target and repeat. Where `Entity` says which identity, `Index` says which iteration. It does not sort anything.

glossary.syntax: SF announce(label: string, value: int) { emit @E { … } }
glossary.meaning: A named sequence of emits that runs inline. It never returns: `-> T` is VS0105 and `return` is VS0107.

glossary.syntax: fn fib(n: int) return int { … return … }
glossary.meaning: A function that computes and returns a value. It can be called in any expression, and across bundles when shared.

glossary.syntax: builder Button { label: string   markup = "<button>" + label + "</button>" }
glossary.meaning: A reusable template. Its members are its parameters, with no ( ) parameter list. Its output field decides what it makes. A builder cannot hold statements.
Instantiates a builder, binding arguments by position. The fragment it produces is queued, not written. A leading count repeats it.
The field NAME picks the channel: @Html, @Style, @Script, @Print. With no such field the builder emits @BuilderName. For this reason these four words cannot be parameter names.
A compile-time copy of a shape's fields into a builder's or event's parameters. It attaches nothing: `target $Card` still matches zero identities.

glossary.syntax: builder Unit { $Health $Shield   mark #Unit }  ·  bring Unit(10, 6) as u
glossary.meaning: A builder with a `mark` member builds an identity: bring = spawn + attach each shape + mark. `as` binds the identity it built.
Fixes some of a base builder's arguments BY NAME and inherits its marks. A fixed parameter takes no argument. A cycle is VS0239.
`?` fills every remaining slot with its default, or a typed zero when there is none. `base` fills one slot with its declared default without skipping it.
A First-Class object that ASSEMBLES. It hears fragments and emits the finished artifact, such as the @Response page.

glossary.syntax: bridge Sync { hear @Hit as h { emit @SyncedHit } }
glossary.meaning: A shard-like First-Class object that spans a boundary. It shows up as Bridge.Sync in `veinc graph` and in provenance.
The module. `by author` roots its qualified name. It is private by default and can span files (publicators/*.vein is API, shards/*.vein is behaviour).
A publicator is a bundle's API grouping. Only `shared("label")` members can be used from another bundle. The label is shown in completion, and over 160 characters is VS0243.

Names the bundle this one is built on. It lets bare names resolve (lookup order: local → built-in → need) and links the bundle into an app. With `as`, names are imported qualified only (*M.…). `use` is retired (VS0338).
A reference that cannot collide: *Author.Bundle.Publicator.member. It is used for includes, cross-bundle emits, calls and discovery. target and mark take bare names.
A manifest listing bundles. The first `load` is the principal and the only one that boots. Every loaded bundle's shards join ONE runtime.
A bundle's boot event, at most one per bundle. It replaces the default @Request { path }. It can be overridden with `--set k=v` or `load … start { … }`.
A block that runs with a given probability. `30%` is a single token. It lowers to random() < 0.30 using a seeded generator, so runs are reproducible.
Branches by NAME, on an enum case or a #Mark. Arms cannot be string literals, so routing on a web path uses `if`.

glossary.syntax: shape $Match { enum State { Kickoff, Play, Over }  state: State }
glossary.meaning: The states a field can hold. An enum can only be declared inside a shape (top level is VS0102). A case evaluates to its own name.

glossary.syntax: repeat 3 as r { … }  ·  while i < 10 { … }  ·  break  ·  continue
glossary.meaning: Counted and conditional loops alongside target. There is no for/in/loop.

glossary.syntax: target $Row #Row by Row.rank as r { … }  ·  ordered by &Card.rank { bring … }
glossary.meaning: `by Shape.field` sorts a query when it is read (stable, strings compared ordinally). `ordered by` sorts brings, which is how fragments and data rows get ordered.
This process's own console address. One program acts out several roles across windows.

glossary.syntax: attach $Parent to crate { of: platform }  ·  t.World.x
glossary.meaning: A parented $Position is local. The runtime composes the chain and publishes $World, which holds absolute coordinates.

rules.rule: A newline ends a statement, so a continuation must END the line it continues from (a trailing + or a trailing ,).
There is no != and no ! at all: inequality is not (a == b) and negation is not x (VS0006). Logic is written in words.
} else { goes on ONE line; an else starting its own line is VS0104 (match arms are exempt).
A string literal is one line; the escapes are \n \t \r \\ \"; a literal newline inside quotes is VS0003.
Lexer keywords are reserved in expressions but most are still legal as field names. RULES says 63; the lexer has 62 today, so check the map before choosing a name.
rules.example_wrong: builder Clock { target: string   line = "clock " + target }   // VS0104: the field declaration is fine, reading bare `target` in an expression is not

rules.rule: A builder's OUTPUT FIELD NAME decides what it makes: markup→@Html, css→@Style, code→@Script, line→@Print, a mark member→identity, inherited→what the base builds, none→@BuilderName.
So markup, css, code and line cannot be parameter names; doing so reports VS0205 at every call site and nothing at the declaration.
A mark member makes a builder an identity template: bring = spawn + attach each shape + mark.
bring X(…) as name binds the identity a template built; as on a fragment builder is VS0221 and it cannot combine with a count (VS0222).
A variant (builder BigCoin from Coin { value = 5 }) fixes a base's arguments BY NAME and inherits its marks; a cycle is VS0239 and an unknown base is VS0238.
A $Shape include is a compile-time field expansion and bring attaches nothing, so a target on that shape matches zero.
Arguments bind positionally across includes in declaration order; ask veinc scaffold <file> '&Name' rather than counting.
spawn() is the only way to make an entity; with no spawn the world is empty and every target matches nothing.
spawn is immediate; attach, unattach, mark, unmark and destroy are DEFERRED to the commit point after the folds.
A structural change is invisible inside the event that made it; seed worlds in run once.
…but the NEXT event sees it, because commit is per event; run once commits once for all shards, and wiring and rendering cannot see each other within one @Request.
A nested target binds BY NAME, so both the outer and inner bindings are readable in both runtimes.
rules.example_right: target $Deck as d { target $Card as c { … d.Deck.title … c.Card.face … } }

rules.rule: folds reconciles concurrent writes (two hp -= 1 give hp - 2); only settled sees the reconciled value, so death checks belong there.
folds ACCUMULATES across ticks and does not recompute; a child can write its parent's component through a handle (c.Parent.of.Deck.count += 1).
$Parent makes $Position LOCAL and the runtime publishes $World before settled; anything reading world coordinates asks for $World.
target binds ONE shape set per loop (several shapes is an AND), and nothing can ask an identity which shapes it carries.
Query order is spawn order unless `by Shape.field` sorts it at read time (stable, strings compared ordinally).
Index is the nearest loop's 0-based counter; it counts position in yield order and does NOT sort.
ordered by &Builder.$Shape.param { bring … } sorts the BRINGS, which is how fragment output (most of a web page) gets ordered.
ordered by also takes a target loop, which is how DATA gets ordered; only bring is reordered.
$Enemy and #Enemy are different things: a different keyword and a different sigil, and a program may use both.
Components unify by bare name across bundles, and a shape cannot include a shape (VS0007); a field mismatch is VS0220 or VS0332.
A shape may BRING marks, which arrive and leave with it in the same commit.
A mark is just a name unless declared; a bundle that declares any mark has its mark names checked (VS0218).
Only shared("…") inside a publicator crosses a bundle boundary; everything else is bundle-private.
The qualified *A.B.P.$Shape / #Mark form is for INCLUDES and DISCOVERY; target, mark, audience and match take a bare name.
An IMPORTED $Shape becomes a real component once something attaches it; target it by its bare name.
The shared("…") string is a LABEL shown in the completion row; over 160 characters is the VS0243 warning.
need "Author.Bundle" names a dependency, widens bare names (lookup order: local → built-in → need) and LINKS the bundle; use is VS0338, a missing author is VS0339 and an unknown bundle is VS0340.
need "Author.Bundle" as Y imports QUALIFIED only (*Y.…) and widens nothing; this is the answer to a VS0216 ambiguity.
A bundle can span files (publicators/*.vein for API, shards/*.vein for behaviour); fragments merge BEFORE the main file, and an API declaration in a fragment is VS0321.
An event is Author.Bundle.Name while a shape is just its name; runtime and stdlib events (@Request, @Print, @Ticked) keep bare names.
An SF runs INLINE (its brings land where you called it); a shard hearing an event does not.
bring and emit QUEUE, they do not write; the queue drains only after every handler of the current event has finished.
veinc serve gives every request a fresh interpreter, so run once re-runs per request; veinc render is the same pipeline, one-shot.
Under Git Bash, pass MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 for a / argument, or the path becomes C:/Program Files/Git/.
There are four checks guarding different things: dotnet test (behaviour), check-ir.sh (IR shape), check-backend.sh (backend meaning), check-perf.sh (speed).
JSON crosses the boundary with fromJson(text) and toJson(shape); integral numbers parse as int, malformed input is null, and both are interpreter-only.
When measuring the backend, use Release on both sides and measure past JIT warm-up.
Arity and literal types are checked (VS0204, VS0228, VS0227, VS0229, VS0230); nothing else about a value is, and a missing value reads as empty, not zero.
target rows as row: $Row declares what OUTSIDE data looks like, so fields are checked and read directly (row.title); an unknown shape is VS0233.
rules.example_right: target rows as row: $Task { bring Task(row.id, row.title, row.rank, row.done) }

rules.rule: A character is a one-character string: no char type and no 'a' literal; two strings compare ordinally.
rules.example_right: fn isDigit(c: string) return bool { return c >= "0" and c <= "9" }

rules.rule: Splitting is done by the host: split keeps empties, lines strips \r, words drops empties, plus chars and trim; all return lists.
Conversions are named after the type (int, float, string, bool) and are total (int("abc") is 0); guard with isNumber.
rules.example_right: if isNumber(typed) { let n = int(typed) } else { … }

rules.rule: Ordering decides in three steps: both text → ordinal; both numeric (parsed text included) → numeric; otherwise ordinal on text, never silently zero.
A file is an event and a failure is a message: @ReadFile answers @FileLoaded or @FileMissing, and there is no catch.
Route file events by tag, not by path; a tag is a mark checked in when arms, so a typo is caught at compile time as a VS0218 warning (in a bundle that declares its marks).

refusals.missing: C-style typed parameters such as `int v` (and mixed `hp : int` / `int v`)
refusals.instead: `name: Type` everywhere: `fn clamp(v: int, lo: int, hi: int) return int`, `let x: T = …`
refusals.why: One rule that reads left to right. Leaving out `: Type` is then naturally just `let x = …`.

refusals.instead: `if` / `else if` / `else`. `when` is only the arm keyword inside `match`.
refusals.why: Identity comes from shape/shard/target, not from renaming conditionals. `when` is kept for match arms.

refusals.instead: `target coll as x { … }` for any collection or query, `repeat N [as i] { … }` for counting, `while cond { … }`, plus break/continue
refusals.why: `target` unifies iterating data with querying identities, which is the central IOP verb. The language reads as targeting sets rather than running C-style loops.

refusals.instead: Compound assignment (`self.Health.hp -= 1`). When several shards write one field, the shape declares a reducer: `hp: int folds sum`.
refusals.why: It separates the per-shard write from the merge policy, which is declared once on the data. The result is deterministic and independent of shard order.

refusals.instead: Data in `shape` (component), `type` (plain value) and `event` (message). All behaviour in `shard`.
refusals.why: The data/behaviour split is what makes folds, deterministic scheduling and parallelism possible. Web and desktop are modelled as identities + shards too.

refusals.missing: A function that both emits and returns, or an `SF` with a return value
refusals.instead: `fn f(…) return T { return … }` for values; `SF f(…) { emit … }` for named emit sequences (`-> T` on an SF is VS0105, `return` outside an fn is VS0107)
refusals.why: 'Returns a value' versus 'emits events' can be decided from the declaration alone. Purity cannot be checked, so a 'verified pure' promise could not be kept.

refusals.instead: A newline ends a statement (a virtual terminator). To continue an expression, end the line with an operator or comma.
refusals.why: The lexer's newline terminator (CanEndStatement) was kept, and blocks use braces.

refusals.instead: `self.Health.hp` (name the target binding) and `*Author.Bundle.Publicator.member` for cross-bundle references
refusals.why: `::` carried two unrelated meanings, and both already had a better spelling. `M::x` had zero uses in samples/ and stdlib/.

refusals.missing: List mutation: append, sort in place, push
refusals.instead: Build lists with `[a, b, c]` or with split/lines/words/chars. Use `len`, `xs[i]`, `target xs as x`, `pick`, `join`. Order with `ordered by` or `target … by`.
refusals.why: Lists exist as values you can build, index, measure and iterate. Mutation has not been designed yet.
Deferred and low priority. Built-ins are special-cased in v1.

refusals.instead: Declare the enum inside the shape that owns it: `shape $Match { enum State { Kickoff, Play, Over }  state: State }` (top level is VS0102)
refusals.why: State definitions stay next to the data they constrain, with no floating global enum namespace. Meaning attaches to identities.

refusals.instead: `not x` and `not (a == b)`. The parentheses matter: `not x == y` is `(not x) == y`, and VS0008 warns about it.
refusals.why: and/or/not are already words, so a symbolic exception would be inconsistent. A dropped `!` flips a condition and still compiles. This is also the general rule: 'C does it' is not an argument.

refusals.missing: Descending order and sorting by more than one component field
refusals.instead: `target $Row #Row by Row.rank as r { … }`: ascending, stable, strings compared ordinally
refusals.why: Sorting at read time keeps entity ids stable, so references to rows are never disturbed. Only ascending order on one field has been built.

workbench:
**VeinScript Workbench**: a desktop IDE (Avalonia). Start it with `dotnet run --project src/Vein.Workbench` or install it with `VeinScript-Workbench-win-Setup.exe`, which installs per user under %LOCALAPPDATA% so the samples stay editable. The first launch opens on the samples, and **Help ▸ Browse Samples** gets back to them later.

**Worth showing on camera:**

- **▶ runs what the file declares.** The file's header line (`// veinc run samples/entities_chance.vein --ticks 4`) becomes an editable command box in the toolbar, so you can change `--ticks 4` to `--ticks 40` and press ▶. Each session shows its exit code and duration (`exited 2 · 1.4s`) and has ↻ to re-run and ⤓ to save the full log.
- **Compile as you type.** About 450 ms after you stop typing, red underlines appear and the Diagnostics list (filterable by severity and text) refreshes. **Quick fixes** exist only where the fix is mechanically certain: VS0228 inserts `?`, VS0218 declares the mark, and VS0338/VS0339 rewrite `use Movement` into `need "kit.Movement"`.
- **Sigil completion**: `$` shapes, `#` marks, `@` events, `&` builders, `*` qualified names, `.` members. Typing `?` right after `emit @E` or `bring B` **expands into the full field list**, with each field's type and the `$Shape` it came from. A signature-help strip marks the current slot in a `bring`.
- **Navigation across bundles**: F12 (it works on a `need` line too), Shift+F12 to find references, Ctrl+T to search symbols, Ctrl+Shift+F to find in files, the Outline pane, and Alt+←/→ to go back and forward.
- **Runtime panel: the killer demo.** A tick stepper, an event timeline and an entity browser. Boot the world, step one tick at a time, and watch identities and their components change. This replaces a line debugger, because shards never call each other.
- **Execution tab** (the `veinc exec` model): each block gets a badge (◆ Event, ◉ Reactive, ◷ Scheduled, ▣ Frame, ∞ Continuous) plus ⚡ parallel / 🔒 synchronized / ! conflict, laid out in waves. It shows that `folds sum` is what makes two shards safe to run in parallel.
- **Events tab**: who emits and who hears each event, with a jump from every row. It flags events that are emitted but never heard, and heard but never emitted.
- **IR Tree / Raw IR**: double-click a node to land on the source line that produced it.
- **Terminal**: several concurrent sessions, each with its own stdin. **Run All Participants** (Ctrl+F5) starts `control_center.vein`'s Control → Alpha → Beta in header order. The **Consoles** topology shows who addresses whom and flags unresolved sends in red. **Live** shows the bound pipes, and **Transcript** interleaves all sessions with timestamps.
- **Preview** for websites: a route picker built from the site's own `if r.path == "…"` conditions, the rendered markup with status and headers, Open in Browser, one-click `serve`, and live reload.
- **Project Explorer** for an `app.vein`: ★ marks the principal and 📦 its dependencies. The **Bundle Inspector** shows a PUBLIC/SHARED/PRIVATE bar. The **Symbols** tab lists every primitive under the author and bundle that brought it, with collisions highlighted.
- **Build ▸ Publish Executable** (runs `veinc build`), **Run Checks** (check-ir.sh, check-backend.sh, …) from a menu, and **New Project** templates for a CLI app, chat app or website.
- The UI also has an **Assistant** panel (sign-in; every suggestion is compiled before an Insert button is offered) and a **Lounge** panel (a shared chat room). They are not described in docs/WORKBENCH.md, so check both live before putting them in the video.
- Not there: an embedded web view (C1b, deliberately left out; Open in Browser covers it).
